#9052. Oregon and Virginia Sue Elon Musk’s SpaceX for Promoting CSAM

Oregon and Virginia Sue Elon Musk’s SpaceX for Promoting CSAM

Oregon and Virginia have filed separate lawsuits against Elon Musk’s SpaceX, alleging that the company violated state consumer protection laws by promoting AI tools that generated sexualized images of women and children without their consent.

The lawsuits, filed in state courts on Monday, name both SpaceX and X Corp., the subsidiary responsible for the social media platform X (formerly Twitter). SpaceX acquired Musk’s company xAI in February, taking ownership of Grok, the chatbot and image-generation tool at the centre of the allegations.

Introduced last year, Grok Imagine included a feature known as “spicy mode”, which allowed users to generate sexualized images and videos from existing photographs.

The states allege that SpaceX promoted the feature to attract users and gain a competitive advantage, despite knowing that its safeguards were insufficient to prevent the production of non-consensual intimate imagery and child sexual abuse material (CSAM).

Wired reports that the complaints argue that the company’s approach prioritized commercial growth over user safety. Virginia alleges that the defendants identified “a market opportunity for more profits” in generating sexualized images of real people, including children, and “intentionally released a product that inundated their platforms with CSAM.”

The scale of the activity has been a central part of the legal action. A study cited in Virginia’s complaint by the Center for Countering Digital Hate estimates that Grok generated and posted millions of sexualized images on X between December 2025 and January 2026, including more than 20,000 depicting children.

The states also allege that Grok was released without sufficient independent safety evaluations and that its internal safety instructions were inadequate. According to the complaints, some prompts instructed the system to “assume good intent” and indicated that the terms “teenage” and “girl” did “not necessarily imply underage.”

Oregon Attorney General Dan Rayfield says the company has allowed the creation and distribution of harmful material in pursuit of commercial success.

“It’s no surprise that Grok and X became a haven for perpetrators using AI to create and share child sexual abuse material, because the lack of needed safety measures was considered a feature, not a bug,” he says, per Wired.

The complaints also point to Musk’s public promotion of Grok during the period when its image-generation capabilities were attracting criticism. While users were prompting the chatbot to create images that appeared to digitally remove clothing from people, Musk posted about Grok “hitting #1 on the App Store in one country after another!”

Both states are seeking financial damages, civil penalties, and legal costs, as well as court orders requiring SpaceX to stop practices that violate consumer protection laws. The attorneys general have also indicated that they want the cases to result in substantial changes to the company’s products and safety measures.

#9049. Flooding in southwestern US underlines risks of Trump administration’s reduction of Bears Ears National Monument

The Newspaper Rock petroglyphs are among the archaeological sites within Bears Ears National Monument in Utah Photo: Matthew Dillon, via Flickr

Recent catastrophic flooding across the southwestern US has renewed concerns about the future management and preservation of Bears Ears National Monument in Utah, which is home to a rich concentration of archaeological sites. The concerns follow the Trump administration’s decision to reduce the monument from more than one million acres to around 120,000 acres, reversing Biden-era protections and dismantling its Indigenous-led management structure.

The decision to shrink the boundaries of the protected area and open the site to resource extraction has become a flashpoint as the region grapples with the effects of severe weather, with the recent floods raising questions around the resources available for the preservation of heritage sites. The flooding hit the Four Corners area—which encompasses parts of Arizona, Colorado, New Mexico and Utah—from late October to early November, causing widespread damage to roads and infrastructure.

A spokesperson for the Bureau of Land Management’s (BLM) Monticello field office in southeastern Utah says in a statement to The Art Newspaper that the public lands it manages, which includes Bears Ears National Monument, were significantly affected by flash floods, resulting in major washouts on many primary access roads and rendering some routes impassable. BLM staff have been patrolling the region to assess road conditions and evaluate the status of infrastructure around areas used for recreation.

“Park rangers and archaeologists have also been assessing cultural sites to identify any potential impacts from the flooding,” the spokesperson says. “While storm events of this nature are not uncommon in this landscape and can affect sensitive cultural resources, no immediate impacts on cultural sites have been reported at this time.”

The local researcher and author Ralph “R.E.” Burrillo was in the town of Bluff, Utah, a gateway to Bears Ears National Monument, when the floods started in late October. He notes that the management plan for the new boundaries has not yet been implemented, so nothing has changed other than the “invisible line”. The longer-term implications, however, remain uncertain.

“With a monument in place, there wouldn’t be these wildcat permits for people supposedly looking to extract resources, but these are just exploratory leases,” he says. “The reality is that there isn’t that much energy to be extracted underground in Bears Ears, or people would have been going after it for decades. When anybody says the monument is locking up America’s energy potential, they are lying.”

Other monuments in the region, like the Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument in southern Utah, which has substantial deposits of coal and other minerals like uranium, chromium and copper, have a longer history of conflict over resource extraction. The Clinton administration established the monument in 1996 in part to prevent commercial development of coal extraction. Several companies had acquired coal leases in the region during the 1960s and 70s, although commercial mining never materialised.

Burrillo emphasises that the demarcation of the Bears Ears National Monument benefits two constituencies: resource developers and opponents of tribal stewardship. The Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument and the Bears Ears National Monument are frequently reduced due to a “handshake deal” that grants energy lobbyists access to energy resources from one site and removes tribal jurisdiction from the latter. At this time, the main immediate threat to heritage sites in the region, Burrillo adds, remains tourism, looting and vandalism.

“What the monument did, at least potentially, was create a nexus for funding to be sent to that area for things like interdiction and law enforcement, education and interpretation, trail maintenance and collaboration with tribes,” Burrillo says. “A monument is a conduit for funding to try to protect those resources from vandals, looters and, again, tourists, who, whether intentionally or not, crawl all over the place. Without the monument, there’s no nexus for funding and that’s really a knock-on effect.”

Although flooding could affect archaeological sites, including potentially eroding petroglyphs, Burrillo says that prehistoric sites in the region are of the least concern. The region has historically flooded, with water sometimes rising to 50ft, and its archaeological sites tell a fascinating story of adaptability, with sites like ancestral Puebloan cliff dwellings having been built higher than the water could ever reach. When Mormon pioneers arrived in the region in the 1870s and attempted to establish a town at Bluff, with farms and as an outpost for missioning the Navajo population, they were unsuccessful and eventually moved north.

“When you go back 500 to 2,000 years, the people didn’t have those dams. You simply had this tempestuous river that was famous for flooding more or less constantly, filling miles around the flood basin with water and mud,” Burrillo adds. “The ancestral Pueblo and their ancestors knew it and built above it. For the most part, they treated the river with more respect than we have. The archaeology is in far less danger than the modern infrastructure for that reason.”

Opponents of the plan say Nine Mile Canyon, described as “the world’s longest art gallery”, is too narrow and fragile to accommodate the widened road and increased tanker traffic

The governance and size of the monument have been disputed for years, and Utah Republicans are still trying to block president Biden's 2021 expansion of its boundaries

The Bureau of Land Management is offering a $10,000 reward for information leading to the arrest of those responsible

Legislators in the state are planning legal action in order to allow mining in region that contains 100,000 archaeological sites

#9048. Photographer Captures Caribou Carrying Around a Dead Rival in Its Antlers

Photographer Captures Caribou Carrying Around a Dead Rival in Its Antlers

A photographer captured extraordinary images of a bull caribou carrying its dead rival in its antlers.

Warning: The following photos contain graphic content that some may find upsetting.

Professional freelance photographer Peter Mather documented the astonishing scenes while he was filming caribou rut in the mountains around Whitehorse in Yukon, Canada, last month. During the rut, or mating season, male caribou compete for the chance to mate with females, often fighting each other using their antlers.

The photographer made the discovery after flying his drone to investigate a grizzly bear he had spotted near his camp. Mather initially believed the bear had killed a caribou, but he was stunned to discover that two caribou had locked antlers during a fight, leaving one of the animals dead.

“I spotted a grizzly bear at a location above camp on two separate locations, so I flew my drone up there, as I suspected the bear had killed a caribou,” Mather tells PetaPixel. “I was blown away to see that what actually happened was that two caribou had got their antlers stuck together when fighting and one was broken. A red fox and a grizzly were waiting nearby, patiently hoping to feed on the dead caribou.”

Mather says he watched the bull caribou for three days as it struggled to survive with its dead rival still caught in its antlers, while scavengers fed on the carcass.

“I spent three days watching the caribou. When the bear left, I walked up to the caribou a few times and fed it lichen and left water for him to drink,” the photographer explains. “Every day, golden eagles, ravens, and red fox were slowly picking away at the dead caribou, and it was getting smaller and smaller.”

He adds: “Every once in a while the grizzly bear would try and sneak up to eat, but the caribou would stand up and defend itself with its antlers, even though it had another caribou attached.”

Mather says he returned with a friend on the third day to try to free the caribou by cutting off the antlers of the dead one with a hacksaw, but was surprised by what he found from the animal instead.

“The final bits of the dead caribou had been pulled free of the bull. He only had the head and antlers of the dead caribou attached,” the photographer recalls. “When I approached, the caribou was able to stand up and run. The last I saw of him, he was trotting into the mountain with two heads.”

Mather works exclusively in Northern Canada and Alaska, focusing on long-term photography projects that document wildlife and the First Nations communities that have lived alongside these animals for centuries, often returning to the same locations over several years and using camera traps to capture unusual images.

Although Mather never learned what happened to the caribou, he believes the animal’s resilience and the fact that it would soon shed its antlers gave it a good chance of survival.

“I don’t know if he survived, but I suspect he did,” the photographer says. “He was the most resilient animal I’ve ever encountered, and I believe he would drop his antlers in a week or two anyhow. Bull caribou drop their antlers every year, shortly after the rut.”

More of Peter Mather’s work can be seen on his Instagram account @peter.mather.photography

#9046. Construction underway on Jean Nouvel's landmark opera house in China

Images courtesy of Ateliers Jean Nouvel

French architecture studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel has shared photos revealing construction progress on the giant Shenzhen Opera House, due for completion in China in 2028.

Located on the Shekou Peninsula overlooking Shenzhen Bay, the opera house will eventually be defined by an elongated, wavy roofscape, nodding to the site’s connection to the sea.

Pritzker Prize-winning architect Jean Nouvel’s studio has designed it as a new cultural landmark for the city, with a 2,300-seat concert hall, an 1,800-seat theatre and an 800-seat venue among its facilities.

The construction photos help visualise the scale of the 250,000-square-metre opera house, with its various facilities sprawling out across its waterfront site.

They showcase its main concert hall with its horseshoe-shaped plan, alongside the two smaller performance venues.

Ateliers Jean Nouvel’s design for Shenzhen Opera House was the winning entry of an invited international architecture competition, for which other entrants included BIG, Snøhetta, MVRDV and Kengo Kuma.

Alongside the main performance halls, it will contain a multifunctional theatre with 400 seats, cultural spaces, backstage areas, apartments for performers and offices.

To help further connect the building to the surrounding water, the interior is expected to feature iridescent materials such as mother-of-pearl, also known as nacre.

“The sea will be both around you and over you,” explained Nouvel when the project was revealed in 2021.

“This explains more clearly why the main foyer has to be made of a noble, precious and luminous material that spells the meeting of sea and music and light,” Nouvel continued.

“Using the lustrous white reflections of a nacreous material will be a concrete poeticisation of the meeting of the sea and the auditorium and concert halls of the Opera House.”

French architect Nouvel founded his eponymous studio in 1994. We recently reported on the news that the studio’s La Querola housing development in Andorra, designed with Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos, was damaged in a fire. The project won the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards, which took place last night.

Another landmark opera house recently featured on Dezeen is the Shanghai Grand Opera House, designed by Snøhetta with a giant spiral staircase.

#9045. No Two Copies of Light Lens Lab’s New 40mm f/2 ‘Hua’ Lens Are the Same

No Two Copies of Light Lens Lab’s New 40mm f/2 ‘Hua’ Lens Are the Same

Light Lens Lab’s founder, Mr. Zhou, collected vintage Chinese lenses long before he started his lens (and film and camera) company. His brand’s newest special project, the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 “Hua,” celebrates the best features of those classic optics.

As Light Lens Lab explains, the “Hua” is also a celebration of the company itself.

“We are proud to announce a small, fun, but special project: the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 ‘Hua,'” the company says. “A token of appreciation for all Light Lens Lab patrons and supporters since 2016.”

China has a rich photographic history and has been producing cameras and lenses en masse for decades. Light Lens Lab outlines the timeline and inspiration behind its new lens:

In December 1953, Wang Daheng and his colleagues in Changchun produced China’s first successful batch of optical elements. In the decade that followed, Shanghai produced the Shanghai 58-I, the first domestically produced camera from China, with Seagull twin-lens reflex cameras shortly following. Shanghai’s No. 2 Camera Factory also built the Hongqi 20, a 35mm rangefinder camera to showcase domestic precision engineering. Even now, with most of the company defunct, these companies and their skill set form the backbone of Chinese optical and photographic manufacturing excellence.

Light Lens Lab says it created the new 40mm f/2 “Hua” as a “tribute” to the Chinese manufacturers that came before it. Every copy incorporates select, restored glass elements from Mr. Zhou’s personal collection, making each lens genuinely unique. According to the company, the vintage elements have been cleaned of historical defects and recoated to match their original specifications.

Each “Hua” gives “photographers a chance to make new photographs with glass shaped by an earlier generation of Chinese lens makers.”

As far as PetaPixel is aware, this is the first time a new lens has celebrated sample variation rather than sought to eliminate it. Two different 40mm f/2 “Hua” copies could render the same scene very differently, making the sample images below a less representative of what to expect than usual.

Every 40mm f/2 “Hua” features six elements in four groups, focuses down to 0.5 meters (1.6 feet), and includes a 10-bladed aperture ranging from f/2 to f/16.

The lenses also share an aluminum-and-brass barrel design based on the company’s current 50mm f/2 model. However, Light Lens Lab says it developed a brand-new Black Chrome finishing process for this special release that will carry over to future optics.

Given the design philosophy and unique manufacturing process behind the Light Lens Lab 40mm f/2 “Hua,” these sample photos may not be truly indicative of all copies of the lens.

Orders start today, November 23, with shipping set to begin in December. Light Lens Lab notes that because this is a limited-edition release built with vintage glass elements, it will produce the lens in “small batches as capacity allows.” It is available in Black Chrome and Silver Chrome finishes for $250.

The manual-focus lens comes natively in Leica M-mount, making it easy to adapt to modern mirrorless cameras.

#9044. Chile’s first Anglican church to host a new museum

St Paul’s Cathedral, Valparaíso, Chile Photo: Graciela Ibáñez

One of the most famous churches in Valparaiso, Chile—a meeting point for seamen, merchants, shipbuilders, musicians, artists and engineers during the 19th and early 20th centuries—will soon host a museum celebrating the influence of British immigration on the port city.

St Paul’s Cathedral was the first Anglican church built in Chile, as well as on the west coast of South America. It was one of the first buildings on the hill where British and German immigrants settled after the country’s independence from Spain in 1818.

The cathedral’s neighbour, Destino Valparaíso (which houses the Immigrant Museum), will oversee the church’s management, restoration and conservation as part of a 50-year lease agreement with the Anglican Episcopal Church Corporation of Valparaíso. The agreement will take effect on 30 November. St Paul’s will undergo restoration of its roof, floors, pews and stained-glass windows—a project expected to last at least a year.

“The church was deteriorating and, as a historic monument, was in poor condition,” Eduardo Dib Maluk, the executive director at Destino Valparaíso, tells The Art Newspaper. “We felt the need to restore it and develop a business model like the one we have at Destino Valparaíso.”

St Paul’s Cathedral, Valparaíso, Chile Photo: Graciela Ibáñez

The Dib family bought the building that now houses Destino Valparaíso in 2016. The former German School of Valparaíso, also a historic monument, was built by the local immigrant community. The school operated from 1870 until 1985, when an earthquake damaged the building and classes were moved to the German school in the neighbouring city of Viña del Mar. The Dib family renovated the building, transforming most of its space into a museum that tells the stories of British, German, Italian, Spanish, French and Arab immigrants who arrived in Valparaíso after Chile’s independence.

Since the Immigrant Museum’s opening last year, it has been the most visited place in an area that Unesco declared a World Heritage Site in 2003. The museum recently opened a space dedicated to the history of sports that immigrants brought to Chile—including rugby, cricket, football, polo, tennis and cycling.

Dib plans to incorporate technology and design into the new museum spaces at St Paul’s Cathedral, as he has in the old German School building. “It won't be an extension of the Immigrant Museum," he says. “It will highlight the milestones achieved by the British, who shaped the Valparaíso that was known until the 20th century.” The city was a technological centre driving the country’s development in the 19th century; it was home to Chile’s first bank, observatory and stock exchange.

St Paul’s Cathedral, Valparaíso, Chile Photo: Graciela Ibáñez

St Paul’s was built by the English engineer William Henry Lloyd, who had come to Chile to work on the construction of the Valparaíso-Santiago railway. The church was inaugurated in 1858, at a time of Catholic restrictions on other religions in the country. As a result, the church was built in a discrete style with small windows and without a main door, spire, cross or bell tower. With a single nave and an adjacent hall, the Neo-Gothic style building occupies a whole city block.

Inside, Lloyd used laminated Oregon pine beams attached with nails and screws to form the cathedral’s ceiling arches, an advanced technique at the time. Its stained-glass windows, representative of the British Gothic Revival, include one by Morris & Co. The church’s organ, made by Forster and Andrews in England, arrived in Valparaíso in 1902. An earthquake in 1906 damaged the massive instrument, which was repaired four years later. (The Queen Victoria Memorial Organ, as it is known, has kept the space active, with concerts every Sunday for the past 35 years.)

Over time the city's British community largely migrated to Viña del Mar or Santiago, reducing St Paul’s sources of funding. “This church requires a lot of maintenance and repairs because of the earthquakes,” says Lynn Gray, a member of the board that manages the cathedral. “It's very reassuring to be able to keep its heritage alive.”

As part of the agreement with Destino Valparaíso, St Paul’s will maintain services such as the ordination of pastors, weddings for members of the British community and the Remembrance Service in November.

The National Service for Cultural Heritage financed the project at Casa Mouat in Valparaíso, Chile

#9043. Dutch Watchdog Says Smart Glasses That Record People Are ‘Unsafe’

Dutch Watchdog Says Smart Glasses That Record People Are ‘Unsafe’

The Dutch Data Protection Authority has advised consumers against buying AI-powered smart glasses, warning that the devices pose risks to both users and bystanders.

The authority also found that the glasses could provide dangerously inaccurate information. During testing, one pair told a user that an ambulance had been dispatched in response to a simulated medical emergency, despite no emergency services having been contacted. Another gave dating advice to an adult who expressed romantic interest in a minor. The devices also misread medication instructions and incorrectly interpreted severe weather warnings.

“Glasses that film you unnoticed are already concerning,” says Monique Verdier, Vice Chair of Autoriteit Persoonsgegevens (AP). “Glasses that also give you incorrect advice when someone’s life is at stake go a step too far. AI offers many opportunities, but we must be able to trust that technology. With the camera glasses examined, that trust cannot currently be justified.”

Critics have also questioned whether recording indicator lights provide sufficient warning to people nearby. The AP found that the lights on some models could be covered with tape. The watchdog didn’t reveal exactly which models it tested; Meta is the market leader.

The findings add to growing scrutiny of camera-equipped wearables. In February, reports revealed that outsourced workers had been able to view sensitive images and video recorded using Meta smart glasses.

Meta has also promoted the potential benefits of smart glasses, particularly for people with visual impairments. Its devices use AI to describe a wearer’s surroundings and read text. The AP acknowledged that the technology could be useful for people who need assistance interpreting their environment, but argued that reliability is especially important in these circumstances.

The Netherlands is not alone in considering tighter restrictions. In September, the Norwegian government said it was considering a ban on camera-enabled wearable devices.

#9041. Coman’s T1 Mini ‘One-Click’ Carbon Fiber Tripod Racks Up Over $375,000 on Kickstarter

Coman’s T1 Mini ‘One-Click’ Carbon Fiber Tripod Racks Up Over $375,000 on Kickstarter

Coman bills its new T1 Mini tripod as “the world’s first one-click travel tripod,” and so far, photographers are keen to try it for themselves. Available first on Kickstarter, the tripod has racked up over $375,000 in funding with three days left in the campaign.

While not a household name in the tripod world, Coman has produced a wide range of tripods since its founding in 2010, including relatively traditional carbon fiber models and heavy-duty ones built for video.

The standout feature of the Coman T1 Mini is how quickly it deploys. Users flip a single switch for each of the three legs, located just below the head, allowing the four-section legs to fully extend in one swift motion. They can also collapse just as quickly when finished shooting. Coman claims photographers can unpack the tripod, fully extend it, and mount their camera in just a few seconds—significantly faster than with traditional tripods.

While rapid deployment is the T1 Mini’s headline feature, it also aims to be a capable, versatile carbon fiber tripod overall. Swift setup is great, but a tripod still needs to remain stable and practical throughout a shoot, not just for the first shot.

The T1 Mini features a maximum height of nearly 160 centimeters (62.8 inches), a reversible extending center column, and a minimum shooting height of just 177 millimeters (about seven inches) when the legs are splayed outward. It folds down to 533 millimeters (21 inches) and weighs 1,675 grams (3.7 pounds). Its maximum load capacity is six kilograms (13.2 pounds), which should support just about any camera and lens combination.

The tripod includes multiple accessory mounting points for lights and microphones, along with an optional magnetic quick-release plate for smartphones that can be used alongside a mounted camera. Coman also offers an optional light stand attachment.

Early-bird backers can get the Coman T1 Mini for 30% off, dropping the price from $399 to $279. Coman says the tripod will begin shipping to backers next month and will be available in three colorways: black, silver, and military green.

As evidenced by the hands-on videos on Coman’s Kickstarter page, the T1 Mini appears to be a finished product, making this feel more like an early-access launch than a traditional crowdfunding campaign. Coman says it started working on its one-touch mechanism in 2023 and finalized the design this past summer. Nonetheless, backers should always do their due diligence.

Denoise, Sharpen, and Upscale Wildlife Photos With Aiarty: 49% Off for Black Friday

Wildlife photography often involves compromise. A distant subject, high ISO (the camera’s light-sensitivity setting, which adds grainy noise as it climbs), cropping, and less-than-ideal light can all leave a good photograph needing some careful refinement. A meerkat shot at ISO 3200 comes back speckled with grain. A bird’s eye lands a touch soft. A deer too far away has to be cropped, then enlarged. The trick is cleaning all of that up without the animal looking fake.

Sample photos: licensed stock images from Pexels, processed by the Aiarty team.

Aiarty Image Enhancer is designed for this stage of the workflow. Using AI models trained for different types of images and conditions, it helps photographers improve visible detail, reduce unwanted noise, and upscale an image for a larger output when needed. The aim is to make better use of the information already captured while keeping the result natural.

That suits a photographer with, say, an iMac at home and a MacBook in the field. Since Aiarty runs on your own computer, you can enhance photos offline, even in remote locations, once its AI models are downloaded.

The workflow is short. To enhance wildlife photos, import a photo or an entire folder, choose an AI model and an output scale, then preview the enhanced result before exporting.

The workspace brings the main controls together, with the original and enhanced images available for side-by-side comparison. You can also zoom in to inspect specific areas, which is particularly useful for checking fine textures such as fur, eyes, and other small details in wildlife photos.

For more control, photographers can adjust the enhancement Strength, compare different AI models, and choose between keeping the original resolution or enlarging the image. Single Export and Batch Export options also make it practical to work on individual shots or multiple photos in one session.

Aiarty can be used as a standalone application or added to an existing Lightroom Classic workflow.

After culling and making basic adjustments in Lightroom Classic, photographers can send a selected image to Aiarty through the Edit In workflow for further enhancement, then continue editing or exporting as needed.

Wildlife photography doesn’t always allow photographers to use their preferred ISO setting. This meerkat image, for example, was captured with a Panasonic LUMIX DC-GH6 at 350mm, f/5.9, 1/400 sec., and ISO 3200. The settings made it possible to capture the subject in the available light, but the higher ISO also left visible noise.

For this photo, we used Aiarty Image Enhancer with its More-Detail GAN v3 model (a generative AI model that rebuilds fine texture such as fur and feathers), processing the image at 1x to keep its original resolution.

As the comparison shows, the enhanced result reduces the distracting grain while keeping the meerkat’s fur and the image background looking natural. Aiarty’s Black Friday offer brings the lifetime license to $79.

Even when the subject is captured at a good resolution, slight softness can make a wildlife photo look less defined.

For this white-cheeked turaco photo, we selected 1x processing to refine the slight softness while keeping the original resolution.

The enhanced result brings out more definition in the white-cheeked turaco’s facial features and eye texture. Details around the eyes and beak appear sharper, and the image keeps its original dimensions.

Wildlife subjects are not always close enough to fill the frame. When a photo needs to be cropped or prepared for a larger display, its original resolution may not provide enough detail, especially when the subject already appears somewhat soft.

For this deer photo, we used More-Detail GAN v3 and selected 2x upscaling. This increased the image resolution from 1920 x 1440 to 3840 x 2880.

The 2x result brings out more definition in the deer’s eyes, ears, and fur, making the subject look clearer and more detailed at the larger resolution.

Wildlife photos taken in challenging lighting conditions may have inaccurate colors, uneven exposure, or a lack of contrast.

Aiarty lets you restore original image colors and fine-tune the overall look with adjustments for temperature, tint, exposure, contrast, saturation, highlights, and shadows.

From cleaning up high-ISO noise to refining soft details and preparing an image for a larger output, Aiarty Image Enhancer brings several image enhancement tasks into one desktop application.

Imagine stepping off a long-haul flight, exhausted and slightly rumpled, and walking into the Park Hyatt Tokyo — the hotel made iconic by *Lost in Translation* — and being handed a room key to a suite with floor-to-ceiling views of Mount Fuji. Or picture arriving at the Park Hyatt Paris-Vendôme, where Haussmann architecture frames your every view and the concierge greets you by name. Or standing in the Park Hyatt New York, 25 floors above Midtown, watching the city sprawl in every direction from a room that costs more per night than most people's monthly car payment. Now imagine paying nearly nothing for it. That's the power of the World of Hyatt award chart — and the Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most emotionally resonant redemptions in all of travel rewards. Here's the math that makes the ChooseFI community's collective jaw drop: a single night at the Park Hyatt New York regularly retails for **$1,200–$2,000**. The Park Hyatt Tokyo commands **$800–$1,500** per night. The Park Hyatt Paris? Easily **$1,000+** in peak seasons. Yet every one of these properties sits at **Category 7**, bookable for just **25,000–30,000 World of Hyatt points** per night. At 30,000 points for a $1,500 room, you're extracting **5 cents per point (cpp)** — in a world where most loyalty programs are engineered to deliver 1–1.5 cpp if you're lucky. The CPP range for this sweet spot runs from **2.7 cpp all the way to 6.7 cpp**, meaning even a modest redemption delivers 2–3x the value of a typical points transaction. Why does this gap exist? Because Hyatt uses a **fixed award chart** anchored to categories, not real-time cash pricing. When demand spikes — New Year's Eve in New York, cherry blossom season in Tokyo, Paris Fashion Week — cash rates explode upward while your points cost stays locked. The hotel's revenue management team can't touch your award rate. That's the pricing inefficiency the ChooseFI community is built to exploit. This isn't aspirational travel for the ultra-wealthy. This is FI-minded travel: understanding the system, earning points intentionally, and converting them into experiences that would otherwise require an extra year of saving. A two-night stay at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for 60,000 points — points you can earn from a single credit card welcome bonus — is the kind of redemption that reframes what financial independence actually looks like in practice.

The core insight here is deceptively simple: World of Hyatt prices its awards on a fixed category chart, while Park Hyatt properties punch dramatically above their category ceiling in cash value.

Here's how the Hyatt award chart works: properties are assigned to Categories 1 through 8, with standard award nights running from 3,500 points (Cat 1) up to 45,000 points (Cat 8). Park Hyatt properties — the absolute pinnacle of the Hyatt portfolio, a collection of ultra-luxury city hotels that competes directly with Four Seasons and Ritz-Carlton — fall predominantly into Category 7 (25,000 points/night) and Category 8 (40,000 points/night). But unlike Four Seasons or Ritz-Carlton, which have largely abandoned fixed award charts in favor of dynamic pricing that tracks cash rates, Hyatt has held the line on fixed pricing. This is a rare and increasingly endangered feature in hotel loyalty, which is exactly why the ChooseFI community should be actively using it now.

The transfer path that makes this accessible is Chase Ultimate Rewards. Chase transfers to World of Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio, and the transfer is instant — meaning you can spot availability, transfer your points, and book within minutes. Bilt Rewards also transfers to World of Hyatt at 1:1, also instantly, giving you two powerful earning pipelines into the same program.

This matters enormously for strategy. Chase Ultimate Rewards is arguably the most flexible points currency in travel rewards — earned through cards like the Chase Sapphire Preferred and Chase Sapphire Reserve — and the fact that it flows directly into Hyatt at a 1:1 ratio without any degradation is a genuine gift. 30,000 Chase UR points become exactly 30,000 Hyatt points. No conversion fees, no waiting period, no surprises.

Another critical mechanism: World of Hyatt charges zero fuel surcharges on award redemptions. With hotel awards this is less of an issue than with airline programs, but it reflects Hyatt's broader philosophy of clean, predictable award pricing. What you see is what you pay — taxes and fees on hotel awards are typically minimal.

Now layer in Globalist status, and the value compounds further. World of Hyatt's top-tier elite status (earned at 60 qualifying nights per year) unlocks complimentary suite upgrades at check-in (space available) and free breakfast for two guests daily. If you're a Globalist checking into the Park Hyatt New York and you receive a suite upgrade, you've just added hundreds of dollars of daily value to an already exceptional redemption — and free breakfast at a Park Hyatt can easily run $60–$90 per person.

The booking window is 395 days out, which matters for high-demand dates. The Park Hyatt Tokyo during cherry blossom season (late March to early April) or the Park Hyatt New York around major events will see award availability evaporate quickly. Understanding that you can search and book nearly 13 months in advance is your single biggest tactical advantage for locking in prime dates.

Finally, it's worth understanding what you're getting at the property level. Park Hyatt is not Hyatt Regency or even Andaz — it's Hyatt's true ultra-luxury tier, with butler service, marble bathrooms, curated art collections, and some of the best city-view room designs in the world. The points-to-experience ratio here is genuinely exceptional.

Before anything else, inventory what you have. Log into your Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards account and note your balance. You need a minimum of 25,000 points for a Category 7 Park Hyatt night or 40,000 points for a Category 8 property. If you're planning a multi-night stay, multiply accordingly — 30,000 points per night at a Category 7 is a reasonable planning number that covers most Park Hyatt sweet spots.

Decide which property you're targeting. The flagship three for this redemption are:

Go to hyatt.com and use the hotel search. Enter your destination city and dates. In the rate filter, select "Use Points" to display award availability. The site will show you the points cost per night — if you see the Category rate (25,000 or 40,000), availability exists. Note that peak and off-peak pricing can adjust these numbers slightly, so check a few date combinations.

Search flexibly. If your first-choice dates show no availability, shift by a day or two — award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is released in small blocks and replenished irregularly. Use the calendar view to scan multiple dates at once.

This is critical: do not transfer points until you've confirmed award availability exists on your target dates. Point transfers to Hyatt are irreversible. Once you've found open award space, note the exact dates and room type, then move immediately to Step 4.

If you're using Chase Ultimate Rewards: Log into your Chase account, navigate to "Pay Yourself Back" → "Transfer to Travel Partners" → select World of Hyatt. Enter the amount (in increments matching your need) and confirm. The transfer is instant — your Hyatt account will reflect the points within minutes.

If you're using Bilt Rewards: Navigate to the "Rewards" tab, select "Transfer Points," choose World of Hyatt, and confirm. Also instant.

Return to hyatt.com immediately after the transfer confirms. Search your target dates again, select the award rate, and complete the booking. You'll pay any applicable taxes (typically modest for hotel awards) and your points will be deducted. Print or screenshot your confirmation.

Award inventory at Park Hyatt properties is genuinely limited. If you lose availability between searching and transferring (rare, but possible), call the World of Hyatt member line (1-800-304-9288) — agents sometimes have access to inventory not visible online. Alternatively, set calendar reminders to check again; properties occasionally release additional award space within 30 days of arrival as booking patterns clarify. Remember: the booking window opens 395 days out, so planning ahead dramatically expands your options.

Let's walk through a real booking that illustrates exactly why this redemption has earned its place in the ChooseFI community's hall of fame.

The Setup: Two Nights at the Park Hyatt Tokyo

You're planning a trip to Japan in early April — a shoulder period just after peak cherry blossom season, when the city is still spectacular but the crowds have thinned slightly. You pull up hyatt.com and find award availability at the Park Hyatt Tokyo for two nights at 25,000 points per night.

The Cash Cost: A quick search on the Park Hyatt Tokyo's direct booking page for the same dates shows standard King rooms starting at $1,100/night. For two nights, that's $2,200 in cash — before resort fees or any extras.

The Points Cost: 50,000 World of Hyatt points (25,000 × 2 nights), transferred instantly from Chase Ultimate Rewards.

The CPP Calculation: $2,200 cash value ÷ 50,000 points = 4.4 cents per point — well above the program's already-impressive baseline and squarely in the sweet spot's 2.7–6.7 cpp range.

What You Actually Experience: The Park Hyatt Tokyo occupies floors 39–52 of the Shinjuku Park Tower skyscraper. Your King Deluxe room on the 42nd floor has floor-to-ceiling windows framing the Tokyo skyline — on a clear morning, Mount Fuji appears in the distance like a postcard. The bathroom features a deep soaking tub, Aesop amenities, and heated floors. Breakfast in the Club on the 41st floor is an exquisite affair — if you hold Globalist status, it's included for both guests, adding roughly $60–$80 per person per day in value.

If you've achieved Globalist status, a complimentary suite upgrade at check-in (space available) could place you in a room with panoramic corner views that would retail for $1,800+ per night.

This is the kind of redemption that makes the FI math click in a visceral way. You earned 50,000 Chase UR points — achievable through a single premium travel card welcome bonus — and converted them into nearly $2,500 of genuine luxury. That's the system working exactly as it should.

The Park Hyatt category properties — especially Tokyo and New York — have notoriously limited award availability. The booking window opens 395 days in advance, and for high-demand dates (cherry blossom season in Japan, summer in Paris, New Year's in New York), competitive award inventory can disappear within days of opening. Set a calendar reminder for 395 days before your target date and be ready to search and transfer the same day.

Cash prices at Park Hyatt properties fluctuate dramatically — your points cost does not. The bigger the cash premium on your dates, the higher your effective CPP. Research when local demand spikes and target those windows deliberately.

World of Hyatt points expire after 24 months of account inactivity. This is activity-based expiration — any earning or redemption resets the clock. Don't let a large balance sit dormant. A small hotel stay, a points transfer, or earning through a Hyatt credit card all count as qualifying activity.

This is the cardinal mistake. Chase UR → Hyatt transfers are irreversible. If you transfer 60,000 points and then discover your target dates are unavailable, those points are now stranded in Hyatt — useful for Hyatt redemptions, but no longer flexible. Always confirm award space first, then transfer.

While 40,000 points/night for a Cat 8 property sounds steep, certain Park Hyatt properties in this tier — like the Park Hyatt Maldives Hadahaa — can retail for $2,000+/night, delivering CPP values that rival the best airline redemptions. Don't automatically limit your search to Category 7.

Hyatt does use peak and off-peak pricing tiers that can push Category 7 awards from 25,000 to 30,000 points on high-demand dates. Always check the actual points cost displayed during your specific date search rather than assuming the standard rate applies.

Properties in high-cost destinations like Tokyo, New York, Paris, Sydney, and the Maldives typically deliver the highest cents-per-point value because their cash rates are so expensive. A Park Hyatt Tokyo stay worth $600-$800/night for 25,000 points is a standout redemption.

This redemption is purpose-built for the intentional luxury traveler in the ChooseFI community — someone who has been systematically accumulating Chase Ultimate Rewards or Bilt Rewards points and wants to convert that discipline into a genuinely extraordinary hotel experience, not just a free night at a mid-tier property.

The minimum to play: You need at least 25,000 World of Hyatt points for a single night — ideally 50,000–75,000 for a meaningful multi-night stay. This is achievable through a single Chase Sapphire welcome bonus plus modest everyday spending.

This redemption earns a **moderate difficulty rating**, and it's worth being specific about where the friction lives — because once you understand it, most of the difficulty evaporates. **The earning is easy.** Chase Ultimate Rewards points flow into World of Hyatt at 1:1 instantly, and Chase is one of the most accessible premium rewards ecosystems for new-to-intermediate travel rewards participants. The points pipeline is well-established and reliable. **The transfer and booking mechanics are easy.** The actual process — confirm availability, transfer points, complete booking — is straightforward if you follow the correct sequence. The Hyatt website is functional and the award search is transparent. **The hard part is availability.** Park Hyatt properties are genuinely popular, the award inventory is limited, and the most desirable dates (cherry blossom season, major holidays, Fashion Week) book out fast. This is where most people hit a wall — they discover the sweet spot, feel excited, and then find no availability for their dates. **Three tips to overcome the availability challenge:** 1. **Use the full 395-day booking window.** Plan further ahead than feels natural. If you want Tokyo in April of next year, you should be searching in late March or early April of the current year. 2. **Be flexible by 3–5 days on either side.** Award inventory often opens mid-week when demand is lower. Shifting from a Saturday check-in to a Thursday can unlock availability that doesn't exist on peak nights. 3. **Check repeatedly near the 30-day mark.** Properties occasionally release additional award space as the date approaches. Setting a weekly reminder to re-check your target dates costs nothing. If you're willing to plan ahead and stay flexible on exact dates, moderate difficulty becomes very manageable — and the reward on the other side is worth every bit of the effort.

This sweet spot was last verified over 90 days ago. Award availability and pricing may have changed — verify current rates before booking.

The Park Hyatt sweet spot is one of the most compelling redemptions in the entire travel rewards landscape. Whether it is the iconic Park Hyatt Tokyo, the beachfront Park Hyatt Maldives, or the classic Park Hyatt New York, this sweet spot consistently delivers outsized value. For anyone building a Chase Ultimate Rewards strategy, Park Hyatt should be at the top of the aspiration list.

#9037. SSdH "renegotiates light" in Melbourne warehouse transformation

A double-height glass atrium draws light into the open-plan interior of Tucker, a former warehouse that Australian architecture practice SSdH has turned into a residence and exhibition space in Melbourne.

For the project, SSdH wanted to focus on adaptation over replacement and aimed to work as much as possible with the existing warehouse structure.

The studio designed a raised courtyard, a steel-mesh external stair tower and a double-height atrium to draw more natural light into the 770-square-metre space.

To help retain the character of the former warehouse, SSdH fitted the main entrance into its loading bay and preserved a ghost sign overhead.

The Galvabond-clad entry was designed to act as a “deliberately compressed” holding zone, SSdH said, suspending visitors within a relatively unlit area before opening onto the light-drenched central space.

“Light was a big part of the original brief, with the existing boundary walls, limited openings and previous additions leaving much of the warehouse interior quite dark”, SSdH told Dezeen.

“We liked the idea of being held for a moment, making the shift in scale and light feel more surprising”.

Next to the main entrance, SSdH placed a double-storey external stairway that leads to a roof terrace. This was clad in steel mesh to allow for natural light and views from the first-floor interiors.

The ground floor interior is dominated by a double-height glass and steel atrium that was angled against the original floor plan of the warehouse to let light into the open-plan living area.

“Our approach begins with looking at what’s already there rather than trying to make something entirely new”, SSdH said.

“We were interested in how the building could continue to evolve through smaller adjustments rather than extensive demolition”.

The studio designed the interior of the home to be “continuously adaptable”, with the ground floor able to be used as an exhibition space.

Much of the floor plan is given over to open space, with a curation of select furnishings anchoring it.

In the living area, built-in sofas line the perimeter of the atrium wall next to the courtyard, and are accompanied by an industrial-informed timber and shearling bench by design studio BMDO.

In the kitchen, SSdH added a monolithic travertine island that is complemented by spotted-gum-timber and stainless-steel cabinetry that was fitted against a preserved painted-brick wall.

“Throughout, the material palette is honest, refined and robust, allowing the characters of the original warehouse to remain present”, said SSdH.

A wooden staircase set within a double-height void leads to the first floor, which features wraparound circulation and is home to the private bedrooms and bathrooms.

Spotted-gum and big-river timber cladding was used across cabinetry, extended doorways and flooring, with exposed roof trusses visible throughout. Both bedrooms receive ample light from south and north-facing windows, with the primary bedroom overlooking the atrium and courtyard below.

The main bathroom is fitted with wraparound marble and features a glass brick exterior wall that SSdH added as part of its aim to “renegotiate light” within the existing framework of the warehouse.

“We were drawn to the thickness and form of the glass, which catches, holds and releases light in a way that conventional textured glazing doesn’t quite achieve,” the studio said.

Overall, SSdH hoped to preserve the charm of the original warehouse while creating an adaptable, contemporary space.

Many decisions were “made on site as the building revealed itself”, the studio said.

“We wanted the spaces to remain open to different ways and possibilities of living, allowing the building to adapt without needing to be completely reworked in the future”, it concluded.

Other Melbourne homes recently featured on Dezeen include a studio with a “lantern-like” glass-block facade, a century-old corner shop transformed into a family home and a home comprised of a cluster of red-brick volumes.

#9036. Abu Dhabi markets itself to global elites—can its public art biennial reach local communities?

Shama Al Hamed, I Breathe Through the City (2026), installation view, Abu Dhabi, 2026

The arrival of Frieze furthers Abu Dhabi’s ambitions to become a premier events destination for global elites. Beyond the fair (which runs until 22 November), the coming weeks will see the jetset descend on the emirate to bid on Picassos at Sotheby’s, sit front row at the Grand Prix and Abu Dhabi Open tournaments, and rub shoulders with celebrities and chief executives at the Global Cultural Forum and the Milken Institute's Middle East and Africa Summit.

But a glittering trail of franchised events is unlikely to leave a lasting impact on the local communities that have built Abu Dhabi and will continue to sustain it. Focusing efforts on attracting the itinerant super-rich might also prove short-sighted for a country surrounded by well-armed and hostile neighbours. So, how to engage those who will remain when regional conflicts escalate or the markets turn?

Public art appears to be one strategy, so proposes the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial (until 15 February 2027). Organised by the Department of Culture and Tourism (DCT), the exhibition Home: A Glossary for a Communal Sense of Place has brought 18 works—most of them new commissions—to public sites across the city, with a further four situated in the nearby oasis desert town of Al Ain.

Asunción Molinos Gordo, Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installation view, Al Ain.Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi

“Everyday life is central” to this biennial “both as backdrop and method”, writes its artistic director, Elvira Dyangani Ose, in the accompanying guide. Out in the desert, Iron Age irrigation systems still used today form the basis of Ascunción Molinos Gordo’s rammed earth sculpture Bil Hana wa Al Afia (2026), installed among working farms during the biennial’s run. Back in the city, the ubiquitous infrastructure of cooling vents is brought to the fore by Shama Al Hamed’s installation of fluorescent aluminium ducting, which spill out like entrails from the observation deck of the former industrial port.

Key to a public art biennial concerned with the quotidian is appealing to non-art specialist audiences. This means considering the “many publics” that exist in Abu Dhabi, Dyangani Ose says. Visitors at sunset will see families jumping on Ivan Argote’s see-saw installation and zooming down its animal-shaped slides.

Despite the temporary nature of an exhibition, each edition of the biennial achieves permanence through its acquisition structure. Last edition, 15 works—around half—were acquired by Public Art Abu Dhabi and are now on display across the city. They include a crescent of silver oyster sculptures by the Emirati artist Farah Al Qasimi, referencing the Arabian Gulf’s once-booming pearl diving industry.

The director of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Clémence Bergal, says a similar acquisition round will take place at the end of this edition. “With so many of the biennial’s works being new commissions, it is a great way to collect work that feels deeply connected and responsive to Abu Dhabi,” she says.

Elvira Dyangani Ose, artistic director of the second edition of Public Art Abu Dhabi Biennial

The biennial is not only a tool for engaging Abu Dhabi’s various communities, but for considering how they live with each other. The theme of this year is the unstable and contested definition of “home”, and Dyangani Ose writes in the catalogue that she is interested in how a “communal sense of place” is formed and negotiated by various groups, sometimes of vastly different cultures and material conditions. “Abu Dhabi is a city in which that distinction matters enormously,” she writes. “Communities from across the world share its streets, its coastline, its daily rhythms without sharing the same histories, the same rights or the same relationship to the land.”

The curatorial statement provides a potent line of inquiry in a country where only a small portion of the population—estimated to be around 12%—has citizenship, and in which the working and living conditions of migrant labourers has been criticised by leading human rights organisations.

These issues appear to be broached obliquely in the multiple references to migration and labour throughout the biennial, including in a striking coastline installation by the Ghanaian artist Serge Attukwei Clottey, composed of thousands of interlocking yellow plastic pieces made from Kuffuor gallons—containers that are ubiquitous in Accra and used to transport cooking oil, water and fuel. These Kuffuor installations are Clottey’s signature, and he has spoken widely about how they refer, in part, to the imbalanced relations of labour and resource extraction between African nations and their trading partners. The UAE is Ghana’s third-most important importer, chiefly purchasing gold. Immigrants from Ghana and other West African nations represent an increasingly large portion of the UAE's manual labour force, chiefly working in construction, hospitality and security services.

Yinka Shonibare, Wind Sculpture (TG) III (2026), installationview, Abu Dhabi, 2026.

Image courtesy of Public Art Abu Dhabi, Department of Culture and Tourism— Abu Dhabi

Unsurprisingly considering the emirate's strict censorship laws, little in the show could be openly perceived as critical, at least of the UAE. Dyangani Ose tells The Art Newspaper that there are certain “limits presented by the framework” of a publicly funded exhibition in Abu Dhabi. She adds that "as global subjects", we are all bound within certain limits.

To its credit, the biennial's public setting provides opportunities for conversations that many art institutions in other parts of the world might shy away from. For instance, Yinka Shonibare’s towering metal plume, painted in both his signature Dutch wax patterns and those of Bedouin textiles, serves as a welcome shade structure for outdoor labourers working in the harsh midday sun. "These publics are just as important to take into account as any other," Dyangani Ose says.

Indeed, providing a platform for a diverse and unexpected set of interactions is a vital part of how Dyangani Ose conceives of a communal sense of place, as “making meaning, despite differences, in public”. For the biennial, this might be its greatest impact of all.

#9034. NASA Image of the Day Captures Cancer Cells in Microgravity Aboard the ISS

NASA Image of the Day Captures Cancer Cells in Microgravity Aboard the ISS

Last month, scientists and photographers all over the world competed in the 52nd annual Nikon Small World Photomicrography Competition, revealing an incredible, often unseen microscopic world. Photomicrography has gone to space thanks to a joint experiment by NASA and Encapsulate Inc.

NASA’s newest Image of the Day shows patient-derived gastric tumor samples in extreme microscopic detail, captured as part of the novel Encapsulate-1 scientific study.

The photo, captured last week aboard the International Space Station (ISS), shows cancer cells suspended in microgravity. Scientists at Encapsulate believe that a microgravity-induced model of metastasis may help save early-stage cancer patients and prevent the spread of cancer cells inside the body.

The initiative, developed jointly by Encapsulate Inc., a Connecticut-based medical startup working on biochips, and NASA, received a $3.63 million grant last year through NASA’s In Space Production Applications (InSPA) program. The goal is to better study, understand, and eventually predict cancer cell metastasis in a microgravity environment unique to space.

“This grant represents a bold step forward in how we approach cancer research,” Dr. Armin Rad, CEO and co-founder of Encapsulate, said last year. “We are honored to partner with NASA and explore the unique advantages of space-based research in advancing cancer diagnostics and precision medicine.”

Extensive, highly advanced scientific research has taken place aboard the International Space Station since it launched nearly three decades ago. According to NASA, more than 4,000 experiments have been conducted on the ISS as it orbits roughly 260 miles above Earth.

Many biology and biotechnology experiments—including cutting-edge medical studies—have been performed in orbit. For example, NASA astronaut Christina Koch, who went to the Moon aboard the famed Artemis II mission earlier this year, studied amyloid protein aggregations aboard the ISS that scientists believe may cause Alzheimer’s disease. Fellow NASA astronaut Serena Auñón-Chancellor worked on developing more effective cancer treatments as part of a study with Angiex Cancer Therapy.

Medical treatments take a long time to develop, of course, but it’s entirely possible that the cancer cell research underway aboard the ISS could save many lives down the road. Medical science breakthroughs routinely happen in labs on Earth, but sometimes they happen in space.

#9033. Free Mac Photo Editor Channels Aperture and Lightroom Classic

Free Mac Photo Editor Channels Aperture and Lightroom Classic

PixelLoupe is a free, open-source photography app built natively for macOS that promises many of Adobe Lightroom’s photo editing and asset management tools.

Photographers routinely look for Adobe Lightroom alternatives for their RAW photo organization and processing needs, hoping to avoid Adobe’s subscription fees. On Mac, many also miss Aperture. PixelLoupe aims to answer both calls as a Lightroom alternative that channels Apple’s defunct software.

Billed as “the spiritual successor to Aperture and Lightroom,” PixelLoupe is currently on version 1.4.2 and is compatible with macOS 27 or later. Its overall layout closely mirrors Adobe Lightroom Classic, offering separate Library and Develop modules, a wide array of RAW editing sliders, folder-based hierarchies, local adjustments, AI-powered tools, and presets. The app is built on Apple’s own RAW image engine, Core Image, and its Metal graphics and compute API.

PixelLoupe promises non-destructive RAW processing, organizational features like catalogs and collections, ratings and flags, keyword and IPTC metadata support, and advanced image adjustments. It even lets users import their Lightroom Classic catalogs, preserving valuable presets, camera profiles, and smart collections. Assuming the accompanying .xmp files are present, basic image edits carry over, too. Lightroom users will also find PixelLoupe’s keyboard shortcuts familiar, as they remain unchanged.

Beyond essential adjustments like sliders, tone curves, and HSL controls, the latest version of PixelLoupe includes AI-powered Assisted Culling, one-click subject selection and masking, and AI relighting.

The app also includes more specialized tools, such as photo merging for focus stacking, panoramas, and HDR photography, alongside a web gallery builder for easy online sharing. That is an impressive feature set for a completely free program. Because it is open source, users can also modify and tinker with the software as they see fit.

There are some caveats to consider, though. PixelLoupe is a solo-developer project that launched just last month, meaning its development was almost certainly heavily aided by AI coding tools. The Github page specifically mentions Claude, a go-to AI tool for solo devs. While AI-assisted coding is commonplace even among major, established developers these days, it’s understandable that some users may be wary of upstart projects like this.

The app’s newness also means there is a risk that some features won’t work as expected. On the plus side, it’s free, so trying it carries no financial risk. Open-source photo editing apps have been popular for a long time, and there are plenty of interesting choices on macOS these days, including the well-known app Darktable. Another popular option is RawTherapee. PetaPixel also maintains a guide to the best free RAW editing programs available, which will be updated early next year.

Until then, photographers are welcome to try PixelLoupe to see if it fits their workflow on macOS 27. It’s available through Pixegen and on GitHub.

#9032. Meet Harry Nuriev, Bjarke Ingels' pick for the most influential designer of the next 20 years

Photography by Jenia Filatova unless stated

BIG founder Bjarke Ingels has selected Harry Nuriev for Dezeen’s 20×20 project in partnership with Kohler. In this interview, the New York and Paris-based designer explains how he constantly aims to reinvent himself and his work.

Nuriev established his studio, Crosby Studios, 12 years ago with the aim of shaking up the world of interior design.

“First, it came from this game of rejection,” he told Dezeen from his house in Tuscany.

“Let’s say everyone likes to use wood – I won’t have any wood. If everyone likes beige or brown – I won’t have beige or brown. People are confused with a material, so that’s exactly the material I’m going to use.”

“I’ll bring exterior to interior, interior to exterior,” he continued. “I’ll mess everything. My colours will be inspired by fashion, my texture will be inspired by architecture.”

“You can’t be safe. You always have to risk.”

Over a decade later, the strategy appears to have worked. Nuriev was recently named Designer of the Year at French design show Maison&Objet and has a client list that many designers would envy. Among his recent works are a sofa for Balenciaga, a pop-up store for Skims, a reflecting pool for Gucci and a puffer-jacket-filled virtual sofa for Nike.

Now Ingels, arguably the world’s best known architect, has selected him as the designer that he believes will have the biggest impact over the next 20 years, as part of our new series marking 20 years of Dezeen.

Nuriev established his own studio after freelancing and working on other people’s projects for many years, with the aim of being able to pursue his own creative interests.

“When you work freelance just to pay bills, you don’t really have particular voice,” he said. “You have nothing really too specific to express.”

“I was like, hold on, I actually need to pull all the things together to express myself, whether it’s comfortable for everyone or not.”

At the time he established his studio, Nuriev recalls the interior design landscape being constrained and dominated by a couple of key, predominant styles that he was determined to break out of.

“Twelve years ago interior design was just minimalistic Japanese style or classic,” he said. “Maybe there were some alternative, very vague and obscure styles, but there was literally just two, maybe two and a half camps.”

“I remember that in interior design, and in particular the industrial area, there was no room to express yourself in a fashion or an art way,” he continued.

“[I realised] there is no way that everyone needs to live the same way, have the same living room and sit in the same sofa. I thought that I will create something different.”

It was really a big experiment. In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky

Rather than identify a target market or clients that wanted a particular style, Nuriev simply set out to create his own individually styled interior spaces and objects.

“It was really a big experiment,” he said. “In retrospect, looking back now, I really think I was lucky.”

“By then I had learned classic and traditional way of doing it, so I knew the marble game and wood game and all of the, let’s say, Architectural Digest alphabet. But my idea was that my personal voice, my internal conversation, was very different, I didn’t know if people would like it or not,” he continued.

“Then, to my surprise, some people liked it.”

Much of Crosby Studio’s work utilises stainless steel, and has an appearance that is cold and almost uncomfortable. However, although this aesthetic is now associated with the studio, Nuriev is keen to ensure that his work continues to evolve.

“I understand we’re responsible for this whole stainless steel, futuristic, uncomfortable, Instagramable aesthetic,” he said.

“In a certain way we keep in our DNA our signature things that people already liked, even though they’re kind of retired for me and maybe I want something different,” he continued.

But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project

“But we always experiment because that’s the part of the formula, part of the recipe, to always have this little spice in every project.”

His metallic, almost cold aesthetic is partly born of the idea that you can create spaces that people can be enjoy without necessarily being comfortable.

“It’s bullshit because there’s no such a thing [as comfort],” he said. “I remember after a nightclub at 2am, sitting on a sidewalk, eating some hot dog and being extremely happy, but also I remember being in the most refined, beautiful restaurant, sitting in the most comfortable chair with soft cushioning and feel miserable.”

“I developed this mentality that comfort is actually not really healthy,” he continued. “Sitting comfortably in a sort of like sleeping environment, where you can relax all the way, can pull the strength out of you.”

The competition to create something new and attention-grabbing has intensified in the past 10 years, but Nuriev believes that it is still possible to find new ways of reinventing materials and forms through a process of experimentation and reinvention that he calls “transformism”.

“[I tell myself] ‘don’t fool yourself, you can’t create anything new, Harry,'” he said. “What you can do, you can find an existing thing and you can reinvent it. You can find a new life.”

“I’m trying to find new materials, and it’s becoming harder and harder because we explore quite a lot of different things, but surprisingly, there is always something,” he continued.

“It’s like music – every year there is new songs, there is new combinations of the same notes that we have known since Mozart, Bach and Chopin, but it’s still different.”

After more than a decade, Nuriev has a clear idea of his and Crosby Studio’s strengths, as well as the limitations of his creations.

“They are dessert-ish in their nutrition level, kind of like the entertaining side,” he said. “You don’t expect a full meal from Crosby.”

“You come to experience emotion,” he continued. “You want to have this sweet or salty or spicy something, and then you get it and you go. It’s not a daily situation.”

He believes that his work translates best at the medium scale – an installation, store, room or hotel lobby.

My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere

“I think I have found my scale,” he said. “We work in big development projects, which is fine. We can deliver it easily, but there are so many great people who can do it better than us.”

“Rather than we just distribute all our juice everywhere, and then maybe it will have less energy, [for example in] a huge building, let’s just do this lobby so crazy that people will feel the emotion.”

As Crosby Studios has established its reputation, the profile of its clients has risen considerably to include some extremely well known and demanding brands, though Nuriev says these projects can be the most creative.

“The calibre of clients is changing dramatically,” he said. “And you know it’s just like in a computer game, you feel like you’re on a different level, they speak in different vocabulary, it’s just complete different game.”

“Now I’m working with big sharks, and obviously their expectation is different. They’ve been working before me with bigger artists, so it’s also challenging. But this is the challenge of growing.”

Nuriev believes his most important role at Crosby Studios now is to maintain the “rebellious spirit” that it was launched with – something that inevitably becomes harder as a studio grows and the clients change.

“I think the game now is to constantly remind myself that we’re not an Armani Casa with steel, no matter how old we are, and to keep this spirit,” he said.

“I think that’s my job as the founder to remind my team, yes, we have gained professional skills, we know how to talk to people, we know how to draft a contract, we know how to deliver on time, but nevertheless, we still want to keep our rebellious spirit.”

His biggest fear? Becoming a pastiche of himself and rolling out designs in an unchanging signature style.

“My nightmare is to become a replica of my own self and just retire, becoming an established artist who just found his own voice and just puts his signature everywhere. This is not what I want.”

“As Coco Chanel said, once you feel comfortable, it’s the time to change completely. So to reinvent yourself is an exercise, and it’s pretty much my daily life.”

#9031. International photography museum Fotografiska opens in Shenzhen

Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in Shenzhen Bay MixC, an upscale retail and culture complex © SFAP Architectural Photography

The international photography museum Fotografiska has recently launched in Shenzhen, its second space in mainland China, after Fotografiska Shanghai opened in 2023. “The strategy was always to self-fund the first space in Shanghai, and then expand through strategic partnerships for subsequent locations,” says Christian Devillers, the managing director for Fotografiska China.

The organisation, founded in Stockholm in 2010, also currently has locations in the Swedish capital, Berlin and Tallinn; and a new venue, in Oslo, is scheduled to open in 2028.

“Museum-going culture [in Shenzhen] isn’t as deeply entrenched as it is in Shanghai or Hong Kong,” Devillers says, and its art-going demographic skews heavily toward young families and professionals. Fotografiska Shenzhen is replicating Shanghai’s late hours and lifestyle offerings, which draw office workers commuting to the city centres, and its first public day on the 1 October national holiday drew more than 1,000 paying visitors.

The project opened with exhibitions across the 5,300 sq. m facility, including a Shi Guowei solo show and Toiletpaper, showcasing Maurizio Cattelan and Pierpaolo Ferrari’s titular magazine (both until 14 March 2027). They have joined a show of photography award Prix Pictet (until 29 November), the six-artist group show Transcendent Realities (until 1 October 2027) and a Michael Najjar solo exhibition (until 17 January 2027). Subsequent planned events include a show of Hong Kong photographers featuring, among others, Ho Fan (1931-2016).

In Shanghai, even with Fotografiska’s busy traffic, admissions and memberships account for only around 20% of total revenue, Devillers says. The museum instead depends on commercial partnerships, and retail and food and drink sales. Fotografiska Shenzhen’s six-year partnership agreement with landlord China Resources Land aims to draw a profit by year three. The institution has set an initial target of 70,000 visitors for 2027.

Fotografiska Shenzhen is located in the upscale retail complex Shenzhen Bay MixC, which is also home to a new immersive art concept called Base. They join several new and forthcoming cultural projects in the city, which is making a concerted push to raise its artistic profile, such as the recently-opened Shenzhen International Art Museum and Shenzhen Bay Cultural Plaza. This month will also see the long-running Hong Kong fair Fine Art Asia relocate to the mainland city (26-29 November).

#9029. SOM completes first phase of Philadelphia train station restoration

Photography by Lucas Blair Simpson

Architecture studio SOM has completed the first phase of the renovation of the William H Gray III 30th Street Station in Philadelphia, USA, “breathing new life” into the 1930s beaux arts main train hall.

The project saw the renovation of the main train hall, a beaux arts Graham, Anderson, Probst & White building completed in 1931 with a grand limestone facade and Corinthian columns. It serves as a major transit hub for the Northeastern United States.

The hall is on the National Register of Historic Places, greatly restricting the changes that can be made to the structure and its interiors.

Keeping to the historic details, including the art deco chandeliers that hang from the tall ceilings, SOM restored the space with builder Gilbane through renovation and a series of specific interventions.

Chief among these was the moving of ticketing, bag drop-off, and other facilities that had been placed in the main train hall into a little-used northern wing of the building.

“Our restoration and repositioning presents an extraordinary opportunity to leverage the station’s strengths, while breathing new life into this beloved building,” said SOM Partner Colin Koop.

This move freed up more room for seating and through traffic in the main hall.

Working with retail partner Nelson Worldwide, SOM also revamped the concessions in the south concourse.

SOM worked closely with US rail system operator Amtrak on the project, which includes offices for Amtrak in the upper levels of the building.

It is part of a wider renovation SOM announced for the station and surrounding areas in Philadelphia in 2016, which included a number of tall buildings. The status of these new structures is unclear.

SOM noted the efforts in preserving the character of the structure.

“We are preserving its historic character while positioning the station for the next generation of travelers to come,” said SOM Principal Phil Wessell.

“As part of our broader work along Amtrak’s Northeast Corridor, this revitalization reinforces the station’s role as both a vital transportation hub and a defining civic space for Philadelphia.”

SOM also led the renovation of Daniel Patrick Moynihan Train Hall in New York in 2021, with plans for a Penn Station renovation released earlier this year by PAU.
