Join The Club for quick access. Enter your email below and we'll send confirmation, and sign you up to our newsletter.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The HEDDphone DX is an open-back headphone that builds on the incredibly popular HEDDphone D1. It has more sub-bass and a more spiky treble, and that's a double-edged sword. Everyone will appreciate its more confident design and its improved comfort, thanks to a new Capra-created headband. But when it comes to tuning, the DX is a softer, warmer take on the lean, mean neutral D1, and I expect that'll enrage as many as it'll delight. For me, the DX is an exciting, musical set that swaps a little detail and imaging for a more fun sound. But at $400 more than the D1, and with a new Capra-created headband released for the D1 early next year, the DX runs the risk of remaining in its older sibling's shadow.

Why you can trust Creative Bloq Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

In the world of audiophile headphones and in-ear monitors (IEMs), second generations of popular products are thick on the ground. Last year the divisive Grell OAE was followed with the far better-received Grell OAE 2. Last month the ground-breaking Kiwi Ears KE4 got a second iteration.

Price: $1,199 / £999Release: 24 November 2026Driver & housing: 50mm dynamic driver with thin-ply carbon diaphragm (TPCD); open-backMaterial: Polymer and metal chassis, soft fabric suspension strap, replaceable velour ear padsCable: Detachable dual-sided 3.5 mm ear cup connectors; textile-sleeved cables terminated in 3.5 mm (with screw-on 6.35 mm adapter) and 4.4 mm balancedImpedance: 32 Ω (at 1kHz)Sensitivity: 100dB @ 1mWWeight: 310g

So it would be simple to think of the new HEDDphone DX as take two of the best-selling (and my favourite open-back headphone) HEDDphone D1. Simple, but wrong.

HEDD have described it as 'the musical D1', but I think they're playing a risky game. Yes, they took on feedback from their audience, some of whom thought the D1 was a little lean and a touch too clean (not I, for the record). And they also took note of critics of the D1's unforgiving headband (yeah, that thing sucks). But instead of giving us a second take of the D1, I think they've tried to give us the HD 650 to the D1's HD 600. If that was the plan, I don't think they achieved it – but it's a fantastic failure nonetheless.

Big picture: If I were reviewing the HEDDphone DX purely on its tuning, design and comfort, it would be an easy recommendation to all. But the DX costs $400 more than the D1, so it becomes more complicated. To muddy the water further, this January HEDD plans to release the excellent DX headband as a $100 add on for the D1. That will make the D1 far more appealing – and still $300 cheaper than the DX!

So, there's plenty to consider when evaluating the new HEDDphone DX. One thing's for certain: The top spots of my list of the best-sounding wired headphones run the risk of being cluttered with HEDDphones.

Overall, the HEDDphone DX is an exciting, warm open-sounding set, with a very well extended lower frequency, and an immersive midrange. With that lower touch of warmth, it loses much of the crystal clarity of the D1, and some of that higher-end detail. But I still hear a spacious presentation with above-average imaging (the perceived placement of instruments), and enough of what makes the D1 great but with a whopping amount of sub-bass.

HEDD shared a B&K 5128 measurement of the DX with me (above), and it largely replicates what I hear. I definitely hear that slight recession in the 1-2kHz region, and an elevation in 3.5kHz. But for me, the treble's squiggly lines differ ever so slightly (all detailed below). What's clear is that HEDD want the DX to walk the tightrope of warmth and richness, while offering relaxed higher frequencies that give us detail without getting sibilant. And they nail it.

Sign up to Creative Bloq's daily newsletter, which brings you the latest news and inspiration from the worlds of art, design and technology.

This tuning suits diverse music genres and immersive gaming sessions, delivering clean transient speed, rich tonal body, and fatigue-free playback across dense, complex, layered multi-track studio recordings. I absolutely love it for EDM, but it's not peerless when it comes to vocal tracks, as we will see in the competition section below.

Bass: Most open-back dynamic headphones suffer from sub-bass roll-off, and that's generally been seen as a tradeoff for all that open, expansive presentation of music. The DX holds full sub-bass extension to 20Hz, smack in the middle of the new Headphones.com preference bounds on B&K 5128 measurements.

Warmth between 100Hz and 250Hz reaches the upper edge of that preference band, adding body and fullness to bass guitars and kick drums. According to HEDD's literature, the high-excursion carbon driver moves air with low - basically zero – distortion, meaning we get clean separation in the bass during complex musical passages.

Now, I don't really know how much of that is audible to the human ear. What I do know is that the bass is about as big and fun as I can enjoy before things start getting claustrophobic. You see, when bass gets overbearing, lower mids in particular can get swamped by it, and a lot of subtlety is lost. However, what the DX does to combat this is add a treble elevation around 10.5kHz, keeping things from getting too swampy. What you get is a big, detailed, but not bloated bass.

It's a tightrope, but the DX does a fantastic job walking it.

Midrange: With its bombastic bass and sneaky treble (more on that later), the mids of the DX are not really the star of the show. Not at first, at least.

But there's plenty going on. From 300Hz to 1kHz, the lower midrange sounds correct, not coloured, giving vocals, and string instruments solid weight. Then things get fun. Around 1.5 kHz there's a dip that comes across as relaxed, then a spike around 3.4kHz for me, which is only emphasised more due to the following dip around 5kHz.

All of which is to say, I can really crank the volume with the DX, and the upper midrange doesn't punish me for it. There's no shoutiness, and instead I get fatigue-free listening with coherent vocal articulation that's proportional against the rich low-end. What's more surprising, considering this rollercoaster, is that the timbre of the DX is natural sounding.

For my HEDD DX review I played them through the Luxsin X8 and the Chord Mojo 2 DAC/Amps. These pairings provided ample power delivery and headroom for the headphones, maintaining an uncoloured signal path from source to transducer. Music streamed via Spotify Lossless.

Treble is largely relaxed with the DX, trading sharp brightness for a smooth, fatigue-free approach. I hear reduced energy at 7kHz that lowers sibilance on a brightly mixed track like Sweet Old World by Lucinda Williams. That's not to say there's no bite here, but it never gets in the way of the music.

Though HEDD's B&K 5128 graph shows a narrow peak at 9-10kHz from their test pinna, for me I got clean treble extension without any glare. Strings, hi-hats, and room ambience retain a crisp texture over longer listening sessions.

I definitely got a bit of spice around 12 kHz, which isn't punishing, but brings with it some micro details, including the mouth clicks of female singers, as with Erykah Badu's Other Side of the Game.

To call the HEDDphone DX's treble dark is totally wrong. It's balanced, but edges towards modest rather than bright, and I think it'll be enjoyable to a lot of people.

I think the asking price of the HEDDphone DX is a hard sell. Yours for $1,199/£999, the DX enters a crowded open-back tier, and though I think it does well against many of them, thanks to its excellent German assembly, full part replaceability, and a five-year warranty, I think people will be expecting a truly exotic tuning for that price. That's not what the DX is about.

The HEDD DX matches the planar Audeze LCD-X at $1,199 but at half the weight, measuring 310g. It undercuts the Aune AR9000 ($1,399), HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled ($1,449), Focal Clear MG Pro ($1,490), and Sennheiser HD 800s ($1,999.95), but of course we're talking about a lot of different tunings there.

I think one of its strengths is its chic German design, and its matte black and subtle cream white does a lot to make it stand out from the crowd. The comfort is something many of the heavier contenders could learn from.

I think because the DX is not going for a risky, exotic tuning – which wins over fewer yet more ardent fans – it makes sense to compare it in detail to two mainstream, best-selling alternatives: The HEDD D1 and Sennheiser HD 650.

For those that missed it, HEDD shook the audiophile world last November with the release of the exquisitely-tuned HEDDphone D1. It was neutral, it was balanced, and for me it didn't seem to have any weaknesses at all. It wasn't warm, but it didn't come across as overly bright. It was about as lean as I can take it before things start sounding cold and clinical. But there was something about its tonal balance where its neutrality came across as rich (though I'd usually use that word to describe warmer sets). It remains my favourite over-ear, open-back headphone to date.

So, the HEDDphone DX has big shoes to fill. But ultimately, comparing them is like pitting Converse against DMs. They're trying to achieve different things... and yet, since they're coming from the same company, and at very different prices, I think the comparison is required.

The D1 is about clarity without exaggerating any part of the mix. The DX is about a good time – whacking up the bass, cranking up that 10.6kHz region to balance it... basically giving you one of the more refined V-shaped sound signatures in a high end pair of headphones.

Of course they share the same DNA when it comes to design and technology. Both headphones share thin-ply carbon drivers, though as said, HEDD positions the DX as "the experience" and the D1 as "the analyst". But that framing understates the musicality of the D1, which remains immersive and engaging despite its neutral focus.

In practice, the DX adds sub-bass weight, upper-bass warmth, a wider soundstage, and a spike up in the treble, whereas the D1 offers tighter bass and overall more focus. Then there's the price. The 'Refreshed' D1, with the new DX headband and travel case, will sell for $899/£699 in January, while the DX costs $1,199/£999.

For my tastes, and considering the price difference, the D1 remains the one I'd recommend to most people. It has more detail, and due to its neutrality presents music as a massive landscape of sound. The DX is more engaging with its bass and 10kHz shot in the arm, but it's still in its bigger brother's shadow.

However, if you find the D1 too lean, the DX could be what you want.

Both headphones share a warm-leaning, relaxed, largely fatigue-free tuning, but even though it feels neat to make a comparison between the D1 and DX with the HD 600 and HD 650, they're all actually slightly different headphones, with distinct tunings.

The Sennheiser HD 650's sub-bass rolls off from around 90Hz, and even though I think the HD 650's punchy mid-bass is criminally understated by critics, it's still easy to see someone wanting more sub bass than it offers. That's exactly what the HEDD DX does – a sub bass that extends deep to 20Hz.

Their midrange presentations are highlights for both headphones, though in subtly different ways. Both offer rich and realistic-sounding vocals and instruments, but I think the HD 650 offers slightly more forward, honeyed vocals, offering more around the 1-2kHz region than the DX, and less around 2.5kHz, giving a sense of space compared to the DX. The timbre of the HD 650 is pretty unbeatable, but the DX gives it a valiant effort.

The HD 650 is more heavy handed with the upper frequencies, which helps bring texture and grip to the mid-bass that it offers, whereas the DX takes a tamer approach to this region. For me, that makes the DX sound a touch soft, and less striking than the HD 650.

And so, I feel like the DX is actually somewhere in between the HD 600 and 650, rather than neatly comparing directly with the latter.

Though I don't believe it has any impact on the sound profile, it's still worth thinking of the different power needs. The 32ohm DX will run off anything, while the 300ohm HD 650 requires dedicated desktop amplification. Weighing 260g and costing around $500, the HD 650 also remains far more accessible, compared to the still-light 310g but slightly eye-watering $1,199, of the DX. Of course, you have to factor in the far superior build of the DX to the plastic fantastic HD 650.

If you're not going to miss the sub-bass, I'd still recommend the HD 650 over the DX. It's still my favourite out of the two. But if you know the HD 650 has a little too much spice in the upper frequencies, and you're after a soft, rich midrange – and you're willing to pay over twice the price – the HEDD DX should be on your radar.

Rated at 32ohms with a sensitivity of 100dB at 1mW, the DX is super easy to drive. I had no issues running it on my Fosi Audio DS2 dongle DAC.

Looking at price point brethren, unlike the 300ohm Sennheiser HD 800 S or the 94dB HIFIMAN Arya Unveiled, it reaches comfortable listening levels from such portable dongles and modest desktop units. A clean solid-state DAC and amplifier with low output impedance gives you excellent driver control, keeping the DX's elevated sub-bass articulate even during dynamic peaks.

The HEDDphone DX gets 10/10 for build and comfort. It really does excel in these areas, and I feel that this should be the new standard at this price point.

At 310g, it undercuts most rivals in its price point on weight. A built-in soft, silky suspension strap, designed by the king of headband comfort Capra Audio, is as good as it gets, distributing the weight across your head. We also get updated, super soft velour ear pads.

Clamp force feels firm on initial wear and may bother listeners sensitive to that, though it was fine for me across many hours of music and gaming sessions.

I also love the subtle matte charcoal metal finish, and updated indented metal mesh around the outer-ear. Add to that subtle white patterns on the outer-ear, making the HEDD logo come through, and you've got a very pretty pair of headphones here.

For $1,199, I'm glad that the DX comes with modular, user-replaceable parts and a five-year warranty. If the tuning is for you, you can expect this headphone to bring you joy for many, many years to come. Excellent work HEDD!

If you've read this review in full, you'll know it's no puff piece – I've made it clear where I think the HEDD DX is lacking. For example, it's less rich and detailed than the cheaper D1. Its above average timbre still doesn't compete with Sennheiser's HD 650, 20 years its senior and a third of its cost. For a sophisticated V-shape tuning, I think its $1,199/£999 price is steep and confusing.

So why 4.5 stars out of 5? Because the two headphones I've compared to the DX are two of my favourite headphones, and as close to perfect as I've heard.

Taken by itself, I think the DX offers exquisite build and comfort, and sounds fantastic. That half star deduction is because of its price. It's priced so much higher than the (in my opinion) better D1. That's confusing to me. Make them the same price, at least! Make it competitive, HEDD!

If you prefer a little bit more warmth, a far more forceful lower end and less overall clarity up top, then I could imagine that you'd prefer the DX to the D1. But until the HEDDphone DX dips under $1,000, I'm going to find it hard to recommend over the D1.

#8947. Hickey Stages: Understanding and Managing Love Bites Effectively

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Hickeys, or as scientists call them, subdermal hematomas, are love’s graffiti. If you’ve ever scrambled for scarves or turtlenecks, welcome to the kissing booth of knowledge! Join us as we navigate the lifecycle of hickeys, from their eye-catching start to their subtle fade, and learn how to speed up their departure.

A hickey, medically known as a subdermal contusion or hematoma, is simply a bruise that forms as a result of vigorous kissing or sucking on soft skin, typically around the neck. This intense suction causes the tiny blood vessels under the skin, a.k.a. capillaries, to burst and release blood into the surrounding tissues. The immediate result? An unmistakable red or purple mark that gradually shifts to a darker shade as it heals.

From a medical standpoint, hickeys are intriguing. They showcase the skin’s sensitivity and the body’s rapid response to minor vascular injury. Not so romantic when you think about it scientifically, right? But hey, it’s all part of the human experience of showing affection — or something like that.

When you get a hickey, your body starts a healing process that resembles how it deals with other bruises. Here’s a more detailed look at each stage of a hickey’s life cycle.

Immediately after the passionate moment, a hickey appears on the skin, screaming in shades of bright red or deep purple. This initial coloration is due to blood from the ruptured capillaries pooling beneath the skin’s surface in response to the suction. It’s your skin’s way of signaling that there’s been some minor internal damage in that area.

As the hickey begins to heal, it undergoes a whole wardrobe of color transformations, showcasing your body’s metabolic process at work.

Initially, the hickey darkens as the blood begins to oxidize. Then, after a few days, the body starts to break down and reabsorb the blood, so it turns lighter — going from blue to green to brown and, finally, mellow yellow. This rainbow journey reflects the breakdown of hemoglobin, the iron-containing substance in the blood, into biliverdin and bilirubin.

Finally, your hickey starts to ghost you. Over a week or two, depending on factors like your skin type, overall health, how severe the hickey was., and how your body rides the healing waves, the last traces of your hickey fade into nothing.

During this stage, the body’s immune system clears away the remaining by-products of the broken-down blood. White blood cells swoop in like a cleanup crew at a festival, gobbling up and digesting the debris in a process called phagocytosis, while increased blood flow to the area helps to flush out the remnants.

Need a hickey gone yesterday? Here’s how to help your hickey heal. Start with a cold pack — grab a spoon from the freezer or a chilled gel pack and gently press it against your hickey. This will help reduce any swelling and scatter the blood pooling under your skin, which can help minimize that bold bruise.

After using cold treatment for the first 48 hours, it’s time to turn up the heat. Switch to warm compresses to get the blood flowing smoothly again. A few minutes a few times a day invites more circulation to the hickey zone, helping you hustle through healing and clear out the blood remnants more swiftly.

You can also try a dab of comfrey ointment. Research shows it may reduce bruise size and coloration for some peeps.

Caught off guard? A little concealer or foundation over the hickey makes it less noticeable.

Not into makeup? Scarves and high-necked shirts are also great accessories for your camouflage arsenal.

Typically, a hickey will last anywhere from 5 days to 2 weeks, depending on its severity and your body’s healing capabilities.

Communication is key! Let your partner know your feelings about receiving a hickey — some might find it fun, while others may prefer to keep their necks clear.

While generally harmless, hickeys can sometimes lead to complications like skin infections or, very rarely, blood clots. It’s best to keep the affection gentle to avoid any issues.

Hickeys are nothing more than bruises in disguise. They start as bright red to purple love stamps and gradually fade over several days to a couple of weeks. Speed up the process with heat and cold packs or a splodge of comfrey cream.

Remember, the best approach to handling hickeys — like all aspects of relationships — is communication and care. So go forth, love responsibly, and keep a scarf handy, just in case!

#8946. Sid Lee Architecture references "rhythm of the vine" for curved Ontario hotel

Photography by James Brittain (unless stated otherwise)

Canadian studio Sid Lee Architecture has created a curved-glass hotel that takes cues from the burgeoning wine region of Ontario.

The Montreal-based studio recently unveiled The Clayfield Hotel, a 60-room hotel with a restaurant, ballroom and rooftop terrace in Niagara-on-the-Lake.

The rounded 94,000-square-foot (8,732-square metre) hotel sits on a property in the historic village that is being transformed by winemakers.

“The Clayfield was conceived as a new hub for Niagara-on-the-Lake, a place where wine culture and hospitality find a home,” Martin Leblanc, architect and co-founding partner of Sid Lee Architecture, told Dezeen.

“Its layered contours, rounded geometry and rhythmic wood elements translate the surrounding vineyard landscape into a building that celebrates the region’s contribution to Canadian winemaking.”

The hotel was conceived as a pavilion set in the emerging townscape between vineyards and the Clayfield Commons housing development on an agricultural road.

The curved form allows access and connection to its surroundings in multiple directions.

“The hotel acts as a threshold between these typologies, connecting the vineyard and the denser village-like development around it,” Leblanc said.

“Its exterior wood elements recall the rhythm of the vine rows, the layered concrete refers to the clay soil and the reflective glass registers the changing light, sky and seasons.”

The studio said that the organic, natural flow of a hotel is essential to the lasting success of the design.

Working back and forth between the architecture and the interior design, the studio laid out spaces to progress from public to private and back again, integrating moments for visitors to discover the landscape.

“As visitors approach and circulate around the building, it frames changing views of the vines, the plaza and the emerging neighbourhood,” Leblanc said. “The lobby acts as a gateway to the vineyard, while the rooftop terrace reconnects the hotel experience with its broader surroundings.”

Meanwhile, the staircase acts as a connector, transition and centrepiece between the plaza, lobby and upper levels.

“Inside, we chose a palette that speaks to the natural beauty of Niagara’s wine country: walnut panelling, concrete, dark amaranth-coloured leather, greige limestone and woven fabrics,” Leblanc said, calling out the limestone registration desk chiselled from the Niagara Escarpment and the restaurant’s curved bar that resembles the shape of the building.

With mostly Teknion furniture, each space represents a season of the vineyard, from spring in the lobby to winter in the guest rooms with more quiet, reserved furnishings that complete the rooms that fan out from the rounded concrete strata.

Founded in 2009, Sid Lee Architecture has six offices across North America and Europe. The studio previously remodelled its own offices in an I.M. Pei office building, overhauled the interiors of the iconic Fairmont Queen Elizabeth Hotel and created an artisan-inspired workplace for video game designers – all in Montreal.

#8945. Bye-Bye Bites: 14 Ways to Get Rid of Mosquito Bites Overnight

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Wondering how to get rid of mosquito bites overnight? Discover simple home remedies for quick relief. From crushed ice to aloe vera, explore easy solutions to soothe itching and inflammation for a peaceful night’s sleep.

If you’re caught without bug bite cream or ointment, don’t worry — plenty of simple home remedies can provide quick relief. From soothing aloe vera to the calming effects of oatmeal, discover easy solutions to alleviate itching and inflammation so you can sleep peacefully.

Just as you’d ice an injury, icing a bug bite can help decrease inflammation and temporarily numb the pain.

If icy cold treatments aren’t your vibe, you can apply heat instead to soothe your bump.

Aloe vera gel does more than soothe sunburns! It can also help ease bug bites and help them heal.

Baking soda can remove the itch. To make a paste, mix 1 tablespoon of it with a splash of water (not too much). Apply it to your bite as you would zit cream. Keep it on for 10 minutes before rinsing it off.

Did you know basil (yes, like the kind in your pasta) has a rich history as a skin infection remedy? It contains antioxidants that may bring down bug bite inflammation.

To whip up your own basil rub, boil a couple cups of water with 1/2 ounce of dried basil leaves. Cool the mixture before applying it to a washcloth and gently massaging it onto the bite for sweet relief.

You already know apple cider vinegar (fermented liquid from apples) is a huge player in the natural remedy world.

Some people use it to clean due to its antimicrobial effects, and others mix it into food or drinks for its possible health benefits (like helping with blood sugar issues).

Its beauty with bites is that it can help ease burning or stinging while disinfecting your scratchy little bump.

Onion juice (while not delicious) has antifungal and antibacterial properties, which could possibly help ward off infection. Plus, it could make your bite sting less. Just dab a bit of raw onion juice onto your bites. The downside? We’re not sure how well it works … and it’s kinda stinky.

Thyme has been used to help with skin concerns for a long time. You can use it to help decrease irritation by chopping it up and applying the teeny leaves directly to your bite for 10 minutes. You can also boil thyme, soak a cloth in the cooled liquid, and wrap it around your bite.

Peppermint oil may work as an anti-itch agent. Mix it with carrier oil (like olive oil) before applying it to your skin, though!

Another natural anti-itcher and astringent, lemon balm, may be helpful. You can either apply a lemon balm cream or chop up the leaves and apply them right to the bite.

Witch hazel is a natural wonder with many uses for skin concerns such as acne and psoriasis. It can tackle inflammation and burning while helping your bug bite heal.

This herb may work, but the science is a little dicey. On its own, arnica is toxic, so any over-the-counter products you find have been carefully diluted for your safety.

The yummy tea that calms and soothes at bedtime has many other uses, including potentially calming an irritated bug bite. Steep the tea bag for 20 minutes before squeezing it out and applying it to your bite once it’s cooled.

Blend minced garlic with petroleum jelly or fragrance-free lotion. Place the mixture on your bite for 10 minutes before removing it and applying a cool cloth.

Icing the bite for 10 minutes and then placing a mixture of baking soda and water on it for 10 minutes is a strong choice.

Though not tested for this purpose, some people turn to Vicks to soothe mosquito bites. It’s possible that its antibacterial and anti-inflammatory properties could help heal and soothe mosquito bites. But FYI, this product isn’t considered the best defense against mosquito bites.

Some toothpastes are cooling, so that sensation may offer temporary relief. Some people use toothpaste on insect bites since many toothpastes contain astringents, which can help shrink tissues.

Using repellent to prevent bug bites is a good idea. PSA: DEET and lemon eucalyptus oil are safe ways to repel insects.

Mosquitoes are low-key little monsters that cause the most insect bites worldwide. Most bites aren’t serious, but mosquitoes can potentially carry diseases.

Ointments, creams, or simple home remedies can help stop the pesky itch after bites. But remember that some natural substances can cause allergic reactions. That said, it’s always a good idea to do a patch test first.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid (AKA protein building block) that supports your body, from your muscles to your noggin.

It’s a non-essential amino acid, which means your body can make it on its own, so you don’t have to get it from food

That being said, consuming foods high in L-tyrosine or taking supplements could have extra cognitive and physical benefits – here’s what to know.

L-tyrosine is an amino acid that the body produces naturally. Though your bod can prob create enough of the stuff on its own, some research suggests that supplementing with it can boost your mood and help regulate your stress response.

L-tyrosine helps make many vital chemical messengers, such as:

Supplementing with L-tyrosine is believed by some to boost levels of dopamine, adrenalin, and norepinephrine in particular.

Foods naturally high in tyrosine include:

L-tyrosine may improve your memory and mental alertness. Since L-tyrosine increases dopamine availability in your body, experts think it may boost your cognitive performance. In addition to reward centers, dopamine is linked to working memory processes and plays a key role in the brain’s aging process.

In a 2019 review of several studies, researchers found that a higher intake of L-tyrosine was linked to improved cognition. It also improved executive functions like brain flexibility, convergent thinking, and reasoning.

However, researchers noted that L-tyrosine is most effective when dopamine and norepinephrine levels are reduced (which basically means when you feel stressed AF).

Some L-tyrosine supplement companies claim that their products are both mood boosters and antidepressants, but the results are mixed.

L-tyrosine increases dopamine, the feel-good hormone that’s linked to reward processing and also addiction. In general, it’s been shown to be a vital regulator of mood, behavior, and brainpower – so it makes sense that getting enough of it could benefit your mood, too.

However, the research on supplementation of tyrosine for depression is super dated, so it’s challenging to draw any definitive conclusions RN. (Plus, depression is also a super complex condition that involves more than just dopamine depletion.)

And though there are some people dubbing L-tyrosine “natural Adderall” for its purported beneficial effect on ADHD, so far, there’s no research to support these claims yet, either. (Though it *is* true that there seems to be a link between ADHD and altered dopamine levels.)

Phenylketonuria is a rare genetic disorder in which the body can’t properly process another essential amino acid, phenylalanine.

Since those with the disorder may also be deficient in L-tyrosine, some experts think that supplementing with it could help relieve some symptoms like seizures or skin rashes.

However, according to a 2021 review of several studies, there is not enough evidence to say for sure.

The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) considers taking L-tyrosine supplements generally safe.

That being said, it’s not recommended to mix with the following medications:

It’s not advisable to take it if you’re pregnant or breastfeeding.

Research suggests that L-tyrosine supplementation likely benefits your brainpower under stress. It also may benefit conditions like depression, but more research is needed to know for sure.

Like any supplement, it is a good idea to contact your healthcare provider before adding it to your medicine cabinet, especially if you have preexisting health conditions or take medications.

#8943. Nip Slip? The Ultimate Guide to Inverted Nipples

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Inverted nipples face inward rather than outward. Though usually harmless, it’s best to check with a healthcare professional to get shy nips the all-clear.

Nipples come in all shapes, including inverted ones. If yours are more like innies than outies, you’re not alone! Inverted nipples, also known as retracted or invaginated, are common and usually harmless.

Nipples can range from popping out when stimulated to constantly staying retracted. While usually harmless, knowing the causes and potential treatments is wise, especially if there’s discomfort. Keep reading to learn more!

Inverted nipples mean your chest cherries retract inward instead of protruding outward. They can be a genetic gift or something that happens over time.

Often, they’re just doing their own thing, but understanding the different grades can help you know if action is warranted.

Nipple inversion comes in three grades, according to the level of drama. Let’s break it down so you know what’s going on with those inward-facing nips.

Grade 1 inverted nipples are like the shy party guests who need a little encouragement to join the fun. They can pop out with stimulation, like a chilly breeze or a gentle touch.

These are the least inverted and usually don’t cause any trouble.

Grade 2 inverted nipples are a bit more stubborn. They can be coaxed out with some effort, but they’re quick to retreat. They might need a bit more attention, mainly if they cause discomfort or issues with breastfeeding.

Grade 3 inverted nipples are the ultimate homebodies. They’re fully retracted and rarely, if ever, make an appearance. These are the most inverted and might need surgical intervention if they’re causing any issues.

So, why do some nipples decide to turn inward instead of standing out proudly? There are a few reasons this might happen:

Sometimes, you’re born with inverted nipples. Doctors call this congenital inversion.

If your parents or siblings have inverted nipples, there’s a higher chance you might too. It’s like inheriting your mom’s eye color or your dad’s knack for bad jokes — genetics is a big player.

For some new parents, the process of chestfeeding can lead to changes in breast tissue that cause nipple inversion. Your boobs are trying to adjust to their new role, and sometimes, things get a little flipped around!

While this can be temporary, it may also stick around long term.

There are a few other culprits that can cause nipples to go inward. These include:

Remember, if your nipples decide to play hide-and-seek and it’s out of the blue, a quick chat with a healthcare professional is always wise to make sure everything’s A-OK. And if there’s pain, nipple discharge, itchy nipples, or bleeding nipples, do so sooner rather than later.

Several options are available for treating nipple inversion:

Gentle manipulation and massage with your fingers can temporarily draw out the nipple.

While this method can help with mild cases (Grade 1), it often provides short-lasting results and needs to be repeated regularly.

Useful for chestfeeding peeps! Nipple shields are soft, silicone covers that fit over the nipple and help coax the nipples outward, making nursing easier.

They provide gentle and continuous pressure that encourages the nipple to protrude.

These devices create a vacuum around the nipple, gently drawing it out gradually. They can be worn for several hours a day over weeks or months to achieve the desired result.

For more severe cases (Grade 2 and 3), a minor surgical procedure can permanently correct nipple inversion.

It involves making small incisions at the nipple’s base to release the tight tissue pulling inward. It’s usually done under local anesthesia and has a quick recovery time.

If they aren’t causing problems, there’s no medical reason to fix them. It’s a personal choice based on comfort and aesthetics.

Grade 1 and sometimes Grade 2 nipples can pop out with stimulation. Grade 3 nipples typically don’t. They’re super shy!

Yes, inverted nipples can be inherited. If family members have them, you might have them, too.

Inverted nipples are a common and typically harmless condition. They could run in the family, show up after breastfeeding, or result from an injury or infection.

Often, they need no treatment. But if they cause issues or occur suddenly, it’s wise to check with a healthcare professional.

#8942. Cosentino supports architectural creativity with Ēclos mineral surface

Cosentino aims to put the creative freedom of architects and designers front and centre with its Ēclos surface, designed for three-dimensional compositions with refined edges, corners and waterfall ends.

Ēclos is the Spanish brand’s latest mineral surface material, made with advanced methods to emulate the look of natural stone and be free of crystalline silica.

The surface is made with Cosentino’s proprietary Inlayr manufacturing process, which makes the rich and naturalistic veining run through the slab.

This gives Ēclos a premium look, Cosentino explained, and makes it a fitting constituent for the most sophisticated interiors.

According to Cosentino, it is in the junctions and details that a kitchen or room feels resolved and where its architectural character emerges.

“For architects and designers, the section deserves as much consideration as the elevation,” said the company. “The placement of a joint, the treatment of an edge and the relationship between adjoining surfaces shape how a material is perceived.”

“These details establish the architectural language of an element, whether the intention is to suggest a continuous volume or to make its assembly visible.”

Although surfaces are often selected based on their colour or pattern, Cosentino says that full-body design should be just as crucial a consideration, allowing exposed edges and transitions between levels or materials to contribute to building a coherent form.

“With Ēclos, the patterning is constructed within the slab rather than confined to its face,” continued the brand. “That makes the relationship between surface and depth an important part of the design conversation, particularly where edges remain visible.”

“The interest lies not just in the appearance of the material, but in how it can be cut, assembled and brought into a project with adjacent finishes.”

Its fabricators can advise how cutting, profiling, jointing and installation can help a designer’s vision come together.

The process can involve reviewing samples, fabrication drawings and, where appropriate, physical mock-ups.

“The position of a seam or the treatment of an exposed edge can subtly alter the proportions and perceived weight of an element,” said Cosentino.

“The aim is not necessarily to make every joint disappear, but to make each one deliberate.”

“Whether the intention is a continuous volume or a clearly expressed assembly, the junction deserves as much consideration as the surface itself,” the brand continued.

Ēclos launched earlier this year and joins an expanding portfolio of low-silica, high-recycled mineral surface worktops from Cosentino, including Silestone, Dekton and Sensa.

It is suitable for both residential and commercial environments and can be used on worktops, splashbacks, walls and other surfaces.

The first Ēclos collection – Eclectic Veins – incorporates 10 stone-like designs, ranging from ice-white styles to dramatic darks, all made with a minimum of 50 per cent recycled content.

The material is practical for everyday use, withstanding scratches and stains, and is easy to clean and maintain.

It is also resistant to temperatures of up to 220 degrees Celsius, including contact with hot cookware.

To learn more about Cosentino and Ēclos, visit the company’s website.

#8941. anđela zora brnas explores how design can nurture interspecies care

through willow weaving, living structures, and garden-based experiments, the interdisciplinary designer explores how humans can become more attentive participants in the ecosystems they inhabit.

Anđela Zora Brnas November 23, 2026 12 min

Lets imagine. Imagine…that we are living ecosystems living in a living ecosystem. Sharing our lives, bodies and habitat with millions of other organisms. Imagine if we never forgot that. What if we celebrated it? How would our lives, bodies, and habitat feel and breathe?

We, humans, cannot live without trillions of microbes in our gut, inhaling oxygen produced by trees, sunlight waking us up or water hydrating our bodies. Even when humanity thinks it can live without other beings and is self-sufficient, it still turns toward the earth, water, air and sun for its energy, materials, nutrients, and species to extract from and manufacture products for its own survival. The age of Anthropocentrism – where human-centered systems are driven by capitalist colonialist extractive ideologies – is leading life on Mother Earth into destruction and suffering. These man-made systems are driving our humanity to exploit space and land, extract materials and build almost exclusively for humans, while ironically often not even contributing to human lives. Other-than-human species are denied the right to space, materials, choice and agency within the human-centered system- or how I usually call it ‘money/power-centered system’.

There is no question that we are in desperate need of ‘new’ and ‘old’ regenerative ways of relating to and living with other life forms. Posthumanist theories – arising to challenge human-centered worldviews and build systems – propose that we as humans are deeply entangled within the web of life. While some humans are trying to create a better future within our human-centred bubble, often the intelligence of the lived world around us is not acknowledged and included. Now when rivers are crying over the cities, earth is shaking everything and species are disappearing, we are lost and lacking ways of how to relate and collaborate with other beings. What would happen if we start to listen? Maybe even seek help from other beings? Allow to be guided by the rhythms of the ecosystems, rather than pushing the healing onto them as saviors?

More than ever, we are in need of creative, empathetic, vulnerable and deeply sensitive ways of being, where we can practice – again as children- how to exist within this web of life. Cultural ecologist and geophilosopher David Abram calls it ‘more-than-human’ world, referring to  a larger field of earthly life—animals, plants, weather, landscapes, and sensory forces—that humans are embedded within and dependent upon. What would our systems and ways of life be like if humans were de-centered from them and instead rewoven in reciprocal relationships with the more-than-human world?

It can be very daunting to realise how much we don’t know, and how far we separated ourselves from the rest of life. Recognising more-than-human as well as indigenous wisdom while seeking for guidance from them, has never been more important. Indigenous scholar Lyla June opened a new possibility in my imagination with her words: ‘What if the Earth needs us?’ She argues that our human-made systems are wrong, but that we don’t have to be these systems.

I started realising that the healing of my own wilderness; the wilderness of human kind, can only happen when we start to decompose the story of us as individual species and start imagining ourselves as part of the living ecosystems.  What if we decomposed our need to ‘save the planet’ and instead focused on healing and caring for it in collaboration with the more -than-human world? As Indian ecofeminist and scholar Vandana Shiva says: ‘We are not carrying the Atlas. The Atlas is carrying us’. It’s about noticing and learning from deep embodied wisdom that ecosystems around us (yes, even in cities) have while healing our own suppressed nature within our earthly bodies.

freeing the soil from rubble on Earth day 2024, many volunteers | image by Viktoria Chocholovágardens with plants for biodiversity, crafting and eating, 2025 at Kabk in The Hague, Netherlands

In my own process of healing the wilderness as a human and designer, I searched for guidance from plants, trees and animal wisdom surrounding me, while seeking for likeminded human earthlings. By hearing wise words of indigenous scientist and writer Robin W. Kimmerers – who in her book Braiding Sweetgrass reminds us how to practice reciprocity with other life forms and relate to them as our oldest teachers – I felt even more drawn to gardens. A crucial moment was 4 years ago when the co-creation of the student-led Green Office Ginkgo and Makers Garden happened at Kabk, Royal Academy of Arts in The Hague. We all wondered how can we imagine, practice and teach art, design and architecture as part of the cycles of life and seasonal rhythms. But we were not only dreaming – we were co-creating our imagination in real life with soil, plants and species. From seed to plant, from plant to craft and back to soil and life. I started seeing gardens as a common playground where boundaries are blurred between wilderness and crafting, humans and other species, design and process.

After few years of existential crisis – where I couldn’t design out of fear for creating more harm – my struggles and wondering got finally transformed into a research quest(ion) within my graduation work ‘crafting interspecies care’ at Master Inside: ‘What can my caring role/s be, as a human and spatial designer within local ecosystems?’

What started as my graduation project, became a journey of developing and cultivating my regenerative design practice. ‘Crafting interspecies care’ is about collaborative designing and cultivating conditions that create and nurture multispecies care, respect, collaboration and thriving. The values and principles keep me grounded and guide me in the process, while the design can be manifested through many diverse mediums, forms, materials, processes, scales, timeframes, topics…all depending on the context.

I strive to switch from seeing ‘designing with materials as resources’ to ‘collaborating with companion species and their materiality and spirit’. Despite the struggle and problematics of – is it even possible to actually collaborate with another being? – with this approach, I set an intention to practice possible caring and respectful interspecies relations, communication and collaboration.

For some time, I have been discovering ways to collaborate with willow trees within the Dutch landscape and urbanscape. Connecting to their spirit and embodied wisdom was the first step, followed by deep research into the seasonal crafts the willow offers and human-willow entanglement : from willow woven fascine mattresses ‘zinkstuks’ as landscape management, growing architecture and woven vernacular walls, to small seasonal everyday crafts as clogs, basketry, furniture, pigment, charcoal, rope and the medicinal uses of willow bark (a precursor to aspirin). I started relating to willow trees as a teacher, learning space, a wise elder, home, a companion. Throughout the process of building living structures, for the first time in my life i was cutting willow branches – harvesting the material from a living being. I thank the willow with grateful words, hug and promises to harvest and create in reciprocity. Keeping in mind that it’s never a dead material – it was and will always be part of a wider web of life that carries wisdom and stories within itself. This kind of simple but deep and intentional gestures became a ritual that inevitably changed how I design and live. Learning about variety of species that are depended on the willow as their home – shelter, food or material source – and analysing the flows of the willow ecosystem procceses, made me concious of my own actions as a human within it.

workshop of weaving living willow dome at Rietvild Academy with design students | image by Cathelijne MontensZora sitting in the living willow dome at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Georg Prenn

Through trial and error, collaborating with willow trees and non-humans within gardens taught me how important it is to observe, sense and be immersed in a slow-deep-entangled time. It taught me to always be reflective and question the impact on systemic scale. Is it the right time to cut a willow tree? Will this idea really support the ecosystem and other species, or is it just my human perspective (subconsciously) imposing what I want to (or I think I have to) create?

woven willow baskets and structures on a willow ecosystem map made from willow bark pigment | image by Georg PrennZora preparing dried willow branches for basketry workshop at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Georg Prenn

During my residency at art center Mediamatic in Amsterdam, I continued exploring my relation with willow trees and weaving multispecies worlds. Co-creating a small growing dome with willow branches is an ongoing experiment on how to craft and share spaces with other species. Humble in size, it questions the multispecies dynamics within urban public spaces and who has the right to exist, inhabit and create. It invites humans to spend time in the small dome and reflect on themselves as part of an ecosystem. The residency culminated with a storytelling performance called ‘Embodying the willow ecosystem’. A story was being told from a perspective of a willow tree aiming to spark imagination within the human audience. As an act of offering, the woven structures ‘Multispecies baskets’ were gifted to the Mediamatic ecosystem, hopefully providing shelter and nesting habitat for species in cities, while continuing to speculate of possible human caring roles within the ecosystems.

Zora teaching basketry at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Georg PrennStorytelling performance “Embodying the willow ecosystem”, at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Skaiste Venckeviciute

Continuing on the quest of exploring ways to craft multispecies cohabitation and caring relations, a project ‘Living architectures’ is being developed. Designer Akash Kumar, ecologist and anthropologist Tara Neary and I are researching how multispecies building with vernacular techniques of willow and clay in today’s urban Dutch cities, could potentially offer regenerative ways of human cohabitation with other species.

It has never been more urgent to embody a reflective and critical thinking, than in today’s fast driven distanced man-made systems. Designing with and within the ecosystem entails that the overall health of the ecosystem and its species needs are at the core of how we think, relate and design.

Rather than perceiving it as losing and giving up on certain ideas, it’s about choosing life, diversity and companionship. Although more complex, slower and demanding, designing with(in) the ecosystems and with the lifecycle awareness can enrich our humanity in ways we forgot its possible. Recognising and realising that we are part of the interconnected fabric of life, changes everything. Practicing, healing, reviving and rewilding is a long process and journey that requires empathy, humility, bravery, patience and creativity. We are all that, we just forgot how to feel and imagine.

Zora as a willow tree at storytelling performance “Embodying the willow ecosystem”, at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Skaiste VenckeviciuteThe woven stuctures offered to the Mediamatic ecosystem and its multispecies community, at Mediamatic, Amsterdam | image by Anđela Zora Brnas

Anđela Zora Brnas (she/her) is an earthling, interdisciplinary designer, researcher, artist and workshop facilitator, in continuous discovery of her caring role(s) within the local ecosystems she inhabits. She started Studio Zora Wildcraft which  focuses on re-imagining spatial design as a living, nurturing, multispecies practice. Guided by seasonal, embodied, sensory and non-linear approaches, Zora aims to create participatory spatial experiences that foster awareness and nurture possible human caring roles within the complex interconnectedness of the local ecosystems. Zora is currently based between Netherlands and Croatia.

This article is part of designboom’s POSTHUMAN UTOPIAS chapter, exploring what happens when humans are no longer the measure of all things. #8940. Skin in the Game: Is Adapalene or Salicylic Acid Better for Acne?

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

If you have acne, you probably know more about skincare than most people. You might even impress friends with terms like “adapalene” and “salicylic acid.”

But do you know what each treatment does for your skin and if one is better for acne? Let’s find out!

Salicylic acid is a keratolytic agent commonly found in over-the-counter creams, face washes, masks, and gels. While it’s often used for acne, it can also help with dandruff, psoriasis, seborrheic dermatitis, calluses, and warts.

Adapalene, often known by its brand name Differin, is a topical retinoid. It comes in various forms, such as gels, cleansers, and creams. And just like salicylic acid, it’s available over-the-counter without a prescription.

On a chemical level, adapalene and salicylic acid work in different ways to clear acne.

Salicylic acid breaks down a protein called keratin in the outer layer of the skin. Studies show this helps remove the buildup of dead skin cells. It also reduces inflammation in the skin, calming the redness that often comes with breakouts.

Adapalene, on the other hand, is a retinoid. And what, you may ask, is a retinoid? It’s a derivative of vitamin A that attaches to receptors in the skin. Doing so prompts cell turnover to speed up, helping skin regenerate more quickly and lowering the likelihood of clogged pores.

So… what do these differences mean for acne? Both adapalene and salicylic acid can treat skin prone to breakouts (though it’s not recommended to use them together since this can over-irritate your skin).

Which one is more potent may depend on your acne type. Research shows that adapalene was among the best treatments for comedonal acne (aka whiteheads and blackheads), whereas salicylic acid was less effective and more affordable.

Long story short: Your dermatologist can help determine which is the smarter choice for your type of acne.

Studies haven’t directly compared adapalene and salicylic acid for blackheads, but both can help. Blackheads form from plugged hair follicles, and salicylic acid’s exfoliating action can clear clogged pores. Adapalene increases cell turnover, which can also help remove blackheads.

Adapalene is a retinoid. Retinoids are well-established anti-aging agents because they stimulate new cell growth and promote collagen production. Some studies have also shown anti-aging benefits from salicylic acid.

While salicylic acid, due to its exfoliating properties, can help reduce wrinkles, adapalene is generally more effective for addressing aging-related concerns like wrinkles.

Adapalene is an over-the-counter acne treatment — so prescription-strength options may work better. According to the American Academy of Dermatology, some of the most potent acne treatments include antibiotics and isotretinoin.

Adapalene isn’t a magic wand for acne. It may be an ideal choice for some people, but depending on your skin type and sensitivity level, salicylic acid, other OTC products, or even a prescription treatment might be your best bet.

Research shows that adapalene can be just as strong for zapping zits as benzoyl peroxide (another potentially powerful weapon in the battle against acne). A 2024 study, for example, found that 0.1% topical adapalene was as safe and effective as a 4% benzoyl peroxide solution in people of color.

Though adapalene may be an effective acne treatment, it’s not the pinnacle of retinoid strength. Of the four “generations” of retinoids, adapalene is considered third-generation. Fourth-generation retinoids are typically stronger and have higher specificity to retinoic acid receptors in the skin. For this reason, they’re available only by prescription.

Feel free to experiment with adapalene and salicylic acid to see which works best for you — after all, it’s your face! You might find one more effective for your skin. For expert advice, be sure to consult your dermatologist.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8939. Framery's flexible pod subscription tackles office furniture waste issue

According to office pod brand Framery, when companies resize or move, desks and meeting-room furniture often aren’t deemed “worth the cost of moving” and are discarded during the process.

Framery explained that the EU and US discard 11 million tonnes of furniture a year.

Specifically, the brand points to a study for the European Environmental Bureau, which found that in the EU, 80 to 90 per cent of office furniture is burned or landfilled.

According to the Environmental Protection Agency, in the US, less than one per cent is recycled.

Framery aims to tackle this issue with its office pod subscription service, presenting a more environmentally-friendly alternative to disposing of office furniture when a lease runs out, for example.

“The ‘fast furniture’ trend means 80 per cent of furniture ends up in landfills,” said Framery’s chief design officer, Joonas Vartola. “We wanted to create a pod that’s part of the solution, not the problem.”

“Framery pods are built for heavy use, keeping them in the field for tens of thousands of sessions and out of landfills,” Vartola added.

For example, if there’s an increase in staff and more pods are needed, or if an office’s layout changes.

The scheme covers the full range of its signature line pods, from one-person phone booths to meeting pods.

According to Saija Serpola, managing director and founding partner at IR Partners, using the pods has enabled increased flexibility and reduced financial risk when investing in additional office furniture.

“We can terminate, increase, or change the solution as our organisation develops.”

Framery pods are built from mono-materials, including steel, aluminium, glass and PET.

“Our pods with heavy-duty, high-quality materials engineered to withstand wear and tear,” said Vartola. “It’s all about reducing waste, from design to decades of use.”

As part of the scheme, when a change is required, the pods are dismantled, shipped and rebuilt, rather than discarded into landfill.

According to Framery, each pod is designed for disassembly, with all parts replaceable and recyclable. This includes everything from interior panels, glass, upholstery, carpet, ventilation units and seals.

During refurbishment, each pod is restored to as-new condition and delivered to its next office with a lifetime warranty.

“That is a manufacturing question before it is a commercial one, and it is settled years earlier, on the drawing board.”

#8938. Everyone Wants This Unapproved Weight Loss Drug—And Some Have Found a Way to Get It

For all the hype surrounding GLP-1 weight loss medications like Wegovy and Zepbound, these drugs don’t work for everyone. Nearly 17% of people on these medications are considered “non-responders,” leaving them looking for a different solution. But there’s a buzzy new medication waiting in the wings. While it’s not yet approved by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA), people are already seeking it out.

It’s called retatrutide, and it’s a triple-agonist medication, which means it acts on three different receptors in the body. By comparison, Wegovy (semaglutide) acts on one receptor, while Zepbound (tirzepatide) works on two.

Retatrutide is already being hailed as a game changer in an area of health that’s already welcomed plenty of impressive medications in the past few years. In fact, clinical trial results show that it’s so effective for weight loss that some people have dropped out of the trials because they felt that they lost too much weight.

But retatrutide is still being tested in clinical trials. Eli Lilly, which makes reatrutide and Zepbound, hasn’t even submitted the trial results yet to the FDA for approval. So this is still an experimental medication—and versions of it are being sold online for cheap.

Mir Ali, MD, medical director of MemorialCare Surgical Weight Loss Center at Orange Coast Medical Center in Fountain Valley, California, tells SELF that retatrutide is “not really available” for use just yet, short of signing up for a clinical trial. There is no set timeline for when it will hit the market, given that clinical trial results have not yet been submitted to the FDA.

If you’ve struggled with losing weight on a GLP-1 medication or just want to pay significantly less for what appears to be the next big thing in weight loss drugs, it’s understandable to be tempted to add this to your cart. Here’s why doctors recommend resisting the urge.

Retatrutide is similar to GLP-1 medications in a few ways. Namely, it’s used for weight loss and is given once a week through an injection. Like Wegovy, Ozempic, and Zepbound, retatrutide works by reducing appetite and slowing digestion.

But retatrutide has more going on than that. This medication acts on three hormone receptors in the body—glucagon-like peptide-1 (GLP-1), gastric inhibitory polypeptide (GIP), and glucagon (GCG). “This is the first one in the pipeline to work on three different receptors,” says Dr. Ali. “The theory is that the more receptors it affects, the more effective the drug will be.”

The medication is currently in phase-three clinical trials, and it’s had some impressive results that suggest it could be the most effective drug for weight loss yet. The latest clinical trial results show that participants lost an average of 28.7% of their body weight on the highest dose of retatrutide over 68 weeks. By comparison, tirzepatide users lost an average of 15% to 22.5% over 72 weeks during clinical trials, and semaglutide users lost 10% to 15% of their body weight over 68 weeks during clinical trials.

It takes a little detective work, but there are some pharmacies that are selling the drug online.

In fact, this has become such an issue that the FDA issued a press release in early February, stressing that it’s illegal to sell retatrutide (and fellow experimental weight loss medication cagrilintide) right now. That includes picking up the medication from a compounding pharmacy.

“Retatrutide and cagrilintide cannot be used in compounding under federal law,” the release states. “Additionally, these are not components of FDA-approved drugs and have not been found safe and effective for any condition.”

The FDA also noted that its officials have issued warning letters to companies that are distributing these medications.

This is hardly shocking, but doctors really want you to take a pass on using retatrutide before it’s FDA-approved.

“People should wait to take medications until they are approved by the FDA to maximize safety,” Richard Siegel, MD, codirector of the Diabetes and Lipid Center at Tufts Medical Center and endocrinologist at Tufts Medicine Weight & Wellness Center–Stoneham, tells SELF. “All scientific data in animals initially and then humans are carefully reviewed by the FDA for any signals that a medication may be harmful.”

That includes side effects you might experience now or in the future, Dr. Ali points out. Compounding pharmacies have become a gray area. They’re able to legally produce and sell their own versions of popular medications when the FDA-approved versions are in shortage. But technically this is no longer legal once the medications are out of shortage.

But compounded drugs aren’t carefully regulated and may not even have the same ingredients or concentration as the medication they’re designed to mimic, Dr. Siegel says. “While these medications may be safe, there is less oversight in their production,” he says.

Dr. Ali warns against going directly through a compounding pharmacy, noting that it’s safer to work with your health care provider if you plan to go this route. “The worst-case scenario is that you’re getting something unsafe or ineffective,” he says.

But, with all medications, Dr. Ali says it’s best to use the FDA-approved version whenever possible. “It’s going to work in a predictable way, and the side effect profile will be well-studied,” he says.

Dr. Siegel points out that there are a lot of options to lose weight right now. And, if you haven’t had success on one, he recommends talking to your healthcare provider about trying a different medication or strategy. If you haven’t had luck while working with a primary care physician, Dr. Ali suggests seeing an obesity medicine specialist who will be more knowledgeable about treatment options.

“Medications for weight management are a powerful tool that should be used together with a comprehensive lifestyle plan focusing on self-monitoring, optimal nutrition, and an exercise prescription, including both aerobic and resistance components,” Dr. Siegel says. Meaning, people who have the best results do more than take medication—they also focus on nutrition and exercise.

If you’re interested in taking a weight loss medication or your existing treatment isn’t working, talk to a healthcare provider who specializes in this area. “These medications are designed for people with significant weight to lose,” Dr. Ali says. “Most likely, they will need to be taken long-term.” That makes getting a well-vetted medication from a reputable source even more important, he points out.

#8937. Bennetts Associates revives Victorian hospital for University of Edinburgh

Film and photography by Jim Stephenson

The conversion of a Victorian hospital into facilities for the University of Edinburgh, shortlisted for the RIAS Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award, features in this video by photographer Jim Stephenson.

The film forms part of a series being published by Dezeen in collaboration with the Royal Incorporation of Architects in Scotland (RIAS) to highlight the annual award’s 2026 shortlist.

In the video, viewers are introduced to the Edinburgh Futures Institute by London-based Bennetts Associates, which involved the revitalisation of the Category A-listed building to create teaching spaces for the university, including a 450-seat auditorium.

Central to the building’s new function was the opening up of the programme to the public, highlighted by the creation of a public square at its front.

“A large part of the project was, of course, rescuing the building,” studio founder Rab Bennetts said.

“Our mission, if you like, was to come back and reopen that main entrance, give it a sense of purpose again, open up the space to the street and make it a public space.”

Established in 2002, the Andrew Doolan Best Building in Scotland Award is an annual award that highlights Scottish projects, with this year’s winner set to be announced on 26 November.

Comprising three reuse projects, RIAS said this year’s shortlisted projects tap into “important conversations around community, collaboration, retrofit and reuse”. Shortlisted alongside the Edinburgh Futures Institute is the Paisley Central Library by Collective Architecture and the Tarlair Outdoor Pool Pavilion by Studio Octopi.

Last year’s winner was a public park renewed by studios Stallan-Brand and LDA Design.

#8935. Thai Massage Therapy: Benefits and What to Expect

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

Feeling stressed? Whether you unwind with yoga or a relaxing massage, Thai massage combines the best of both worlds, benefiting your mind and body. Here’s everything you need to know!

Thai massage is a special kind of bodywork that blends relaxation with flexibility. Think of it as a gentle, full-body, more active experience. It’s all about boosting your flexibility and energizing your body. Just a heads-up: napping during a Thai massage might be a challenge!

Drawing from Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine, this ancient technique mixes assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and soothing rocking for 60 to 90 minutes. Unlike Western-style massages at a local spa, Thai massage takes place on a mat on the floor. A certified therapist will work to stretch your muscles and apply pressure along your body’s energy lines, known as sen, to release stress with a graceful, rhythmic touch.

You can schedule a Thai massage at many spas, massage clinics, and even some yoga studios, but make sure you find someone with the proper training and certification to give you an authentic experience.

When you arrive for a Thai massage, you might be given some comfy clothes, like a T-shirt and drawstring pants. You’ll remove your shoes, silence your phone, place your jewelry in a small dish, and settle onto a floor mat. Before the session, let the therapist know if you have any injuries.

If this is your first session, it can be intense, so focus on breathing and relaxing. You’ll likely start on your back, with the therapist beginning on your feet and legs. Since the therapist uses their body weight to guide you, it might initially feel a bit weird. Some discomfort is normal as your body stretches, but don’t hesitate to let your therapist know if anything feels uncomfortable.As the session progresses, you’ll likely switch positions, including flipping onto your belly or trying various other postures. Go with the flow as your therapist guides you through stretches and yoga-like moves designed to open up your joints, move your energy, and release tension. Keep breathing and communicate with your therapist throughout the process.

As the session wraps up, you’ll enjoy some gentle rocking motions to ease you out of the massage. You might feel sore afterward, especially if it’s your first Thai massage, so hydrate and rest. You’ll likely feel incredibly relaxed, more flexible, and energized.

Pro tip: Clear your mind and be open to guidance. While the stretches may feel awkward initially, allow yourself to let go. This can help you fully experience the massage’s benefits.

Your Thai massage experience won’t resemble a Western-style deep tissue massage. You won’t be naked under a sheet on a raised massage table, and the massage therapist won’t be using long, deep strokes to work your muscles.The other significant difference is that, like some forms of yoga, Thai massage has a spiritual element based on Buddhism. As they use the weight of their bodies to work on your body, your therapist is also trained to send you kind, loving, healing vibes. The ultimate goal is to help you feel better by allowing your energy to flow throughout your body.

The ancient practice of Thai massage combines assisted yoga stretches, acupressure, and rhythmic rocking to unknot your body and get your inner energy flowing. Unlike Western massage techniques, you’ll be fully clothed on a floor mat, with the massage therapist using their entire body to release your tension.

Permit yourself to let go, and expect an active, sometimes intense, full-body experience that leaves you relaxed and energized.

Last medically reviewed on July 31, 2024

#8934. gerhard richter’s pavilion opens in doha, wrapped in patterns inspired by islamic geometry

six patterned walls, mirrored interiors, and a sculptural tower bring the german artist’s decades-long investigation of abstraction into a spatial experience, drawing connections with the geometric traditions of islamic art.

Gerhard Richter‘s permanent pavilion in Doha, Qatar is now open, conceived as a freestanding work of art and architecture in MIA Park, outside the Museum of Islamic Art. Realized in collaboration with Selldorf Architects, Doha Pavilion: Gerhard Richter houses a collection of the artist’s paintings and sculptures, including works created specifically for the project. The hexagonal structure translates Richter’s exploration of abstraction, repetition, and perception into space, while its patterned exterior draws connections with the geometric traditions of Islamic art (find designboom’s previous coverage here).

The six exterior walls of the pavilion feature decorative patterns derived from Richter’s Abstract Painting (724-4), created in 1990. The artist developed the compositions through a mathematical process that began in 2010, digitally dividing the original painting into progressively smaller vertical strips, eventually reaching 8,192 sections. Each strip is mirrored and repeated to produce a symmetrical horizontal pattern, applied to the pavilion’s exterior. The intricate patterns recall the repeating geometries and interlaced arabesques found in Islamic visual culture, establishing a connection between Richter’s experimental approach to abstraction and the artistic traditions of the region.

Τhree new large-scale works from Richter’s Strip series, which began in 2011, are displayed throughout the pavilion. They translate the original abstract painting into thin horizontal slices, each measuring 0.08 millimeters wide, creating compositions built from fragmented color and repetition. At the center of the space stands STRIP-TOWER (2026), a tripartite freestanding sculpture designed by Richter specifically for the pavilion. Two large, floor-to-ceiling Mirrors, belonging to a body of work the artist began in the 1980s, occupy the narrower walls. Their reflective surfaces capture the artworks and visitors, producing shifting visual relationships and an evolving sense of space.

Outside the structure, a stone sculpture titled Brunnen (Well) extends the installation into the surrounding park. Richter’s idea for the pavilion dates back to a visit to Doha in 2013, when the artist was developing his Strip paintings.

The architecture and history of the city prompted him to consider how different strands of his artistic practice could come together in a permanent structure. ‘My trip to Doha in 2013 came two years into developing my Strip paintings, and the city’s architecture and history sparked an idea for a pavilion that could unite the thematic threads of that body of work,’ the visual artist explains. ‘Doha is the right place and the only place for my Pavilion.’

The project was realized in collaboration with Selldorf Architects and forms part of the legacy of the Qatar-Germany 2017 Year of Culture. Its location in MIA Park places it among a growing collection of public artworks by international artists, including Richard Serra, Nairy Baghramian, and Peter Fischli and David Weiss. According to Qatar Museums Chairperson Sheikha Al Mayassa bint Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani, the pavilion aims to connect contemporary artistic practices with the geometric traditions of Islamic visual culture while making art accessible as part of everyday public life.

The unveiling coincides with the Qatar Creates Fall/Winter 2026–27 program and the inaugural edition of Rubaiya Qatar 2026, an international visual arts quadrennial running from November 21, 2026, through April 30, 2027. Rather than functioning solely as a space to exhibit Richter’s work, the permanent pavilion extends his investigation of abstraction into the surrounding environment. Visitors encounter the artist’s visual language through the building’s exterior, interior installations, and reflective surfaces, experiencing painting not only as an image but also as a space to move through.

#8933. Extra Skin? 9 Exercises for A Sagging Neck

Follow Greatist on our socials for all things health.

We’re not in love with the term “turkey neck” — it’s just extra skin.

If you don’t want to learn to love the extra chin you’re in (though we wish you would!), you can perform some exercises that may tighten your neck muscles.

Though some swear these moves work, there’s no research backing them up, and they can’t zap away extra flowy skin.

Instead, they’re more likely to help strengthen the muscles underneath loose neck skin. Unfortunately, skin removal is usually accomplished with more intense methods, like surgery.

However, these popular neck exercises are simple enough for a test drive and may help tone your neck muscles naturally.

Exercise may be possible to tighten up a turkey neck, but it doesn’t eliminate loose skin like surgery or lasers.

Yes. Certain cosmetic products and procedures — especially surgery — improve loose neck skin the best. These include surgical neck lifts, lasers, Botox, and certain neck creams.

Surgery and other cosmetic methods for turkey neck can offer impressive results.

Are you not into cosmetic procedures or surgery? Neck-toning exercises and facial yoga movements may offer some improvement. However, loose skin is generally not tightened naturally.

Loose neck skin is normal (and honestly v common).

Still, these simple moves may result in toned neck muscles. Just be careful so you don’t wind up with an actual pain in the neck. If you can, it’s best to chat with a healthcare professional first.

#8932. Upside-down cantilever cracks open timber hotel by BIG

Architecture studio BIG has unveiled a hotel building with a stepped, zigzagging design that will function as a “gateway” to the Siegenthalergut urban district in Thun, Switzerland.

Together with landscape architect August + Margrith Künzel, BIG designed the 13,000-square-metre Nachwachsende Stadt (Growing City) development, which will form a key section of the new district.

Nachwachsende Stadt will be comprised of four timber buildings, which will house two hotels, residences and commercial spaces. It will be located on a prominent site in Thun’s new Siegenthalergut district, close to the future Swiss Football Association headquarters.

The most striking of the four buildings is a timber block with a cantilevered corner volume that will be home to both a three-star and four-star hotel.

The stepped design creates terraces that are mirrored by the upside-down design of the cantilevered volume, forming a central rift that will be glazed to let light into the building,

“The Siegenthalergut site is an opportunity to create more than just a new development,” BIG partner Sören Grünert said.

“It allows Thun to grow without losing its character while also raising its profile on the national stage,” he continued.

“With the future home of the Swiss Football Association right next door, the neighbourhood will become the city’s calling card: a community, a gateway, and a landmark all at once.”

The hotel building will have commercial spaces along the street and a rooftop restaurant. It will be complemented by three residential buildings, which will also be built from timber but have a more traditional gridded design.

BIG used timber to help reduce the buildings’ carbon footprint, designing the development for “future disassembly and reuse” so that it can be adapted over time.

The development will also have green roofs, photovoltaic panels and rainwater retention systems to help it achieve a targeted SNBS Gold standard.

Construction on the Nachwachsende Stadt is expected to start in 2028.

BIG also recently designed a “modular blueprint” for Refugee City in Rwanda and the cloud-like Tirana Fountain Plaza above a public park.
